_ VICTORIA. 0 Queen—NY more than Queen-0 woman grand The brightest jewels in thy diadem Grow dim before thy tears. Re-crowned by them • The woman ranks the Queen and doth command A stricken nation's love. The Motherland Seems nearer now, since o'er the ocean's swell Was borne the sound of our sad, tolling bell, And thou and thine mourners with us did stand. God save the Queen"—The Queen and woman, tool errant length of days, a happy peaceful reign, To one who joined with us in sorrow true, • And bowed her crowndd head above our slain. Mencef.rth upon her shield this legend stands: Tis better far to conquer hearts than lands.' --Now York Trthune. A. P. WILLIA-MS.

LIMITS OF HUMANITY. When the eternal Father of gods and men Soweth with kindly hand Forth from the rolling clouds Lightnings of blessing Over the fields of Earth, Humbly, then, I thelast Hem of his garment kiss, With the love and the fear Of a child in my breast. For with the gods May no son of man compare 18fotarsuuephwchnragdt.wheietthernsobaareleastdhh, shine, Nowhere he finds there Place for his foot to stand, And with him freely Sport there the, birds and clouds. When he with strong And marrowy bone stands On the well-grounded Base of tne solid earth, Not even then He dares with the oak c.QMpare. Or with the vine That clambers rctur,d its trunk. Fay what distinguisheth Gods from the sons of men? They are as waves That rolling-on waves flow In an eternal stream; Us the wave lifteth, Us the wave wheimeth. And we are seen no mcro. Small is the ring That claspeth our life round; And generations On generations Coming and going, Add link to link Of an Infinite chain. —Professor Blackie in Blackwood's Magazine for Dec., ISBI.

A petrified woman has been discovered near Halifax. It is suspected that her husband gave her fifty shillings, with- out her asking, to get a new autumn bonnet, and she was petrified with astonishment. . THE SCULLERY.—As much care should be taken with the scullery of a houee as with any other room in the establish- ment. It should be specially well lighted; it should be thoroughly well supplied with hot and cold water; the sinks in it should ha made of enamelled iron and placed beneath the windows; the drains from it should be completely trapped on the outside, unless the main drainage be posi- tively perfect, and the ventilation should be secured exactly in the same way as in the kitchen. The scullery should never be made a receptacle for broken food, vegetable sub- stance, or debris.—Good Words. ROBBERY OF THE ATDIOSPIIERE.—There is a principle of "practical reason"—as momentous as any set forth from Rilnigsberg—that the air by which we breathe and hear is nc man's property, but a public heritage; to be used, as the Roman state jugera, or any other park or "common," under reetrictiens, and abused ' under penalties." We have no more right to Men it by discordant sounds thart to defile it by evil odours; and taking too large a share of it is a usurp- ation. But the unwritten laws of the air, unlike the writ- ten laws of the land and water, are constantly violated with Impunity. Incapable of rhetoric on so grave a matter, I cling to logical divisions. ellobbery of the atmosphere as- sumes two forms—the vai tions we make in it may be too k ' rapid, i.e., we may talk t loud, or they r tinuou3, i.e., we may ta too much may be too con- . . . . Finally, let us venture to remark that what was a forgivable flaw in Ben Jon.son and Samuel Johnson (in PO many respects strangely allied), in Coleridge, and Macaulay, ;and Carlyle, is an 1 ordinary mortals an &pardonable sin, an offence against the elements of manners; that we are no more entitled to seize our neighbour's share of an afternoon than his share of a good dish at a table d'hote ; that all civilised converea- - tion demands reciprocity, the capacity to listen as well as to speak, and a respect for the laws of the game.—" Social .Plagues," in Good Words. MAIOE THE Games Won' —Many mothers, accustomed to bard work themselves, allow their daughters to grow up in comparative kllene s. These unfortunate girls, with no special purpose before them, are in danger of learning only how to dress, to play the piano, possibly to cook a dinner— although that is not very common—but with no more idea that they are important factors in the great plan of humanity than if they were not human beings at all. If ever they do any work in the world through necessity, it is likely to he inefficient and unsystematic work; or if they do achieve anything really good, it is done with the pain and difficulty which those must suffer who work without proper discipline and knowledge. They are not contented and happy, for they have nothing to de with the time, which often hangs heavily mem their hands. SECONDARY BarrEures.--3.1. T. Rousse communicated to \ the Academie des Sciences his experiments for the accumu- lation of electricity. He proposes several forms for secondary batteries, the two following being the most remarkable :—At the negative pole he uses a sheet of palladium, which during .the electrolysis absorbs more than 900 times its volume of hydrogen; at the positive pole he uses a sheet of lead; the electrolysed liquid is sulphuric acid at one-tenth. Another form giving good results is produced by making the nega- tive pole a slender plate of sheet iron, which absorbs more than 200 times its volume of hydrogen when electrolysed in a solution of ammonium sulphate. The positive pole is formed of a sheet of lead covered with a layer of litharge. These plates are immersed in a solution containing 50 per cent. of ammonium sulphate. ACTION OF COW ON THE VOLTAIC 'Ac.—A series of observations of the voltaic arc as affected by a cooling cur- rent of water has been lately made by M. Tommasi, who used as rheophores (i.e., carriers of the current), two U-shaped copper tubes, placed horizontally opposite each other, and traversed by cold water. In these circumstances the luminous power of the arc is considerably weakened, being reduced to a mere luminous point, even when the very intense current of 50 to 75 large Bensens is used. The arc is also very unstable. The least puff extinguishes it. A sheet of paper placed above it at a distance of about one- fifth of an inch acquires in a few seconds a black spot, which extends, and is before long perforated, but the paper is not ignited. The arc is formed of a luminous globule, moving up and down between the reophores. Its form and its great mobility recall the spheroidal state of liquid drops. If the south pole of a magnetised bar be brought near, the arc is attracted and may go out. The north pole has an opposite effect. The quantity of ozone seems to be greater than when the arc is not cooled. In spite of the cooling the flame of the arc is slightly green, showing that a part of the copper is burnt. NEW METHODS IN PORCELAIN MANITFACTIIRE.-The paste used for porcelain often contains ferruginous particles, which give the baked articles a colour, or a mimutely- spotted appearance, where a pure white may have been de- sired. In this way ceramic products may lose as much as 50 per cent, of their value. The attempts hitherto made to remove those traces of iron with magnets have met with poor success. Recently, however, at two important French works, the Faiencerie of Criel, and the establishment of MM. Pillivnyt and Co., of Mehun-sur-Yevre, it was decided to set up powerful apparatus in which the electricity, instead of being supplied from batteries, was obtained by means of a small Gramme machine driven by a steam engine. The arrangement (which is said to work well) comprises a strong horizontal elertro-magnet, with the poles very near each other, and between them a thin box. The paste, very liquid, enters the upper part of this box and is deflected towards the polar tides by a bent piece of zinc. As it flows down these sides, the iron corpuscles are caught on them by the magnetic force. The apparatus is cleaned twice a day, by means of a jet of water, the magnet being unmade. About one gramme of iron particles is stopped in the passage of 12 kilogrammes of paste, and 500 or GOO kilogrammes of paste may be passed through one apparatus in a day. Again, a porous porcelain or earthenware is produced by Herr Buchholz, of Charluttenburg, by mixing the prepared paste with matters which burn while the wares ass baked, and leave the spaces they previously took up empty (except a little ash). Different kinds of matter for the purpose are taken, according to the.kind of pores desired. Sad grains of various kinds and sizes are suitable, especially poor corn; still better, thin rods of willow, birch, or hazel, cut up into small pieces, which are sorted and rounded in a mill. Herr Buchholz also utilises the same principle for producing regular, continuous pores or apertures in porcelain ware by means of wooden rods embedded in particular directions in the paste. MICA MM.—A well-known German manufacturer of mica wares, Herr Raphael, of Breslau, now makes mica masks for the face, which are quite transparent, very light, and affected neither by heat nor by acids. They afford good protection to all workmen who are liable to be injured by heat, dust, or noxious vapours, all workers with fire, metal and glass melters, stonemasons, &c. In all kinds of grinding and polishing work, the flying fragments rebound from the arched mica plates of the mask without injuring them. These plateseare fixed in a metallic frame, which is I well isolated by means of asbestos, so as not to be attacked 1 \ by heat or acid. These masks allow the turning of the eyes in any direction, and, as against mica spectacles, they afford the advantage of protection to the whole face. In certain cases, the neck and shoulders may also be guarded by a 1 sheet of cloth impregnated with fire-proof material, or by I asbestos sheet, attached to the mask. The interval between the mica and the eyes allows of workmen who have poor ' eyesight wearing spectacles, and of workers with fire or in melting operations wearing coloured glass spectacles under the mask, without fear of the breakage of the glass, mica being such a bad conductor of hear. Where the mask has to be worn long, it is found desirable to add a caoutchone tube with mouthpiece for admission of fresh air; the tube passes tint to the shoulders,where its funnel-shaped end (sometimes holding a moistened sponge) is supported. The mask has a , sort of cap attached to it for fixture on the head. I THE GROWTH OF PLANTS IN CARBONIC AClD.—While I plants draw the azotised and mineral matters they require from the soil, they are believed to get their carbon mostly from the airs through the leahs. A new series of observe- tionLas to the effect of greatly increasing the carbonic acid In th'S atmosphere about a plant have been lately made by M. Deherain, who grew young bean, rape, and tobacco plants under capacious bell jars, supplied from time to time with carbonic acid. Other similar plants were grown under bell jars, with ordinary air renewed at intervals. The bean and rape plants did not seem to profit by the excess of carbonic acid • bat it was otherwise with the tobacco, which grew I ' , stronger and more fleshy, though shorter in COe than in ! air. While the leaves of the tobacco grown in air had only a few grains of starch in the chlorophyll cells, there was an extraordirary profusion of these grains in the leaves of the other plant; and the grains were of large size. The vege- table matter elaborated by the tobacco in CO, was proved to contain more carbon than was contained in the CO2 intro- duced. Whence this carbon in excess? M. Deherain elves reasons for believing that the carbon of organic matters of the soil was metamorphosed into CO, by the oxygen of the air in the bell jar, and that this was diffused in the atrwosphere, so that the leaves could utilise it.

......... _ CULTURE, &C. A farm in South Wilts changed hands recently, the new lenant paying £2OO for a farm which had, until then, been let at £5OO. The rent of a farm on the estate of a noble marquess in North Wilts, which bad been let at £670 prior to the recent bad seasons, has been reduced to £315, the same tenant remaining in occupation. RENT ote IMPROVED FARMS.—A tenant-farmer writes to ask advice under the faillowing circumstances :—He took a farm in a very poor state eight years ago, at the high rent of 40s. per acre, other land in the district being now let at 163. an acre. He has greatly improved the farm, in proof of which he states that in the first year he had only 16i bushels of wheat per acre, 20 bushels of barley, and other crops in proportion; whereas this year he got 39 bushels of wheat per acre, 41 bushels of barley, and 48 bushels of oats. He has asked for a reduction of rent, or compensation for improvements; but his landlord refuses to yield to either demand. He wants to know whether he can legally claim compensation, or whether he should stop another year. If he is a yearly tenant, and has not agreed to contract him- self out of the Agricultural Holdings Act, he can claim com- pensation, but not otherwise. As to whether he should stop in the farm another year, that depends upon circumstances, which no one who is not well acquainted with them can estimate.—Mark Lane Express. AGRICULTURAL DEPRESSION IN Eforalarn.—England does not possess a monopoly of landed depression. Grazing land in Friesland, "the garden of Holland," which, a few years ago, was worth from 2,500 to 4,000 gulden per hectare (LB3 to £133 per acre) and was letting at £6 and £8 per acre, gradually declined in 1879, then fell with amazing rapidity (nearly 50 per cent.), and now from £2 to £3 is the annual rental of this same land. An English agriculturist on the spot says the cause of the depreciation is American produce put upon the market at prices which " stopped all competi- tion." When land was realising high prices in Friesland, some enterprising English merchants obtained a concession for reclaiming some thousands of acres forming the rich bed of a shallow lake. No sooner had the concession been ratified than it became a marketable commodity, so great , was the confidence of those who were aware of the transaction. ' The scheme was tempting, for the surrounding land was selling (when it was sold) at upwards of £lOO per acre. The English engineers estimated the cost of the reclamation at £4O the hectare, leaving a net profit of £6O per acre. The works were completed and the land was reclaimed, pumping stations erected, and all was hastening to completion, but in proportion to this progress was the decline in the value of land in the best parts of Holland, so that on tffectual completion the laed—a rich virgin soil—was not worth one- third its estiroated value, or enough to pay off the amount raised on mortgage.--Land. DRESSING FOR SEED CORN.—As the open weather con- tinues and wheat has this year generally returned more money per acre than barley, there may be a disposition on the part of some farmers to sow a little more wheat. How- ever favourable December may prove for such late sown wheats, vegetation must be very slow, and all birds and ver- min are extra sharp at Christmas, which makes valuable the receipt for dressing grain which was furnished some years ago by Mr. Jas. Howard, M.P. Hooka may come upon the field so dressed for a day or two, but after trying a grain or two they do no further harm. For Eight Bushels of Wheat.--; pint gas tar, 21b. blue vitriol, 2 gallons water or more, according to the time of year, tem- perature, ecc. How to Use.—Put the tar and vitriol into a galvanised Iron pail, pour on two gallons boiling water, and well stir the whole until the tar is dissolved. If scum rises, skim it oft with a whisp of straw or a piece of bagging, to either of which it will readily adhere. By the time the tar is dissolved, the liquid will be cool enough to be poured over the corn, which should be well turned in the heap two or three times, so that all the 1 kernels get snore or less soaked. Barley requires nearly one-eighth more tar than wheat, and does not require quite so much vitriol. When corn is very dry, the water may be increased in quantity to nearly 3 gallons. Peas and beans may be dressed with the same preparation, but care must be taken that the corn gets well impregnated and not simply smeared, for it is the taste imparted which deters rooks and other birds from taking it. STORING TURNIPS.—III storing turnips, every precaution should be taken not to place them too many together; or, if this is done, to afford proper means of ventilation, as turnips when stored heat prodigiously, mad unless this be done they are liable to ferment no much as to perish that way. Small heaps are best, with shafts up their middles when they are covered up by earth in the fields, and such shafts can easily be formed by small bundles of straw. Some farmers also place swedes and turnips;between rows of wattles, which are roofed on the top and thatched over. When the roots are brought to the homestead to be stored, the latter is no doubt as good a mode as can possibly be adopted, provided, of course, a supply of wattles is forthcoming to strike up for banks of about 71t. or 8f t. to be formed between them. The worst thir g which can be done is to bank them against walls or the earth embankments often found on the borders of fields. The roots nearest these impermeable structures in- variably decompose owing to the heat drawing thither and finding no escape. The Scotch and North-Country men have other and more economic methods of preserving turnips from frost sevetity, by forming trenches with the plough between every third and fourth row, and lifting the roots and throwing them into these trenches, and then ploughing two deep furrows over them. When this is done, turnips are considered to stand much more weather severity than they would have done standing in the fields. EXPERIMENTS on ParaToes.—Experiments bearing on , the growth and preservation of potatoes are always'of in- terest. To ascertain the infience of moisture on the yield of potatoes was the object of an investigation recently made by Herr Birner. Twenty vessels were filled with the same kind of garden soil, and arranged in five series of four vessels each. Each series contained a different proportion of moisture to the others, but in all other respects the treat- ment was identical. In these vessels the tubers were grown, and they were found to ripen first in the soils containing the most water, and in those containing the lowestpercentage of water not till 18 days after the first. The difference of pro- duce was enormously in favour of the potatoes plantel in the moister parcels of soil, and the investigator thinks that when the necessary plant food is present, the dampness of the soil exercises a very decisive influence. This conclusion Is obviously quite independent of the fact that a very wet season is most favourable to potato disease. From the same German source as the foregoing, we learn that diseased potatoes, even if badly attacked, can be used as cattle food. They are best cut up small, boiled or merely scalded, mixed with chopped straw or chaff, and stored in narrow trenches covered up with clay; so stored they will keep many years, we are told • but this we are inclined to doubt. Messrs. Rohl and Hess believe they have discovered a means of preventing store potatoes from succumbing to disease. When taken from the ground they are left in a weak solution of calcium chloride, one part to 1,000 of water, for half an hour; they are then transferred to a soda solution of the same strength, after which they are washed in clean water and dried in the air. One pound of chloride of calcium and the same quan- tity of soda are enough for 500 pounds of potatoes. DANISH SWEET CREAM BUTTER.—The butter made in Denmark is held in high esteem in Europe, on account of its keeping qualities. How it is made is described in a recent number of The Mach Zeitung, the method given being that followed at one of the largest factories in Den- mark, as follows :—The special aim at this factory is the production of the finest quality of sweet cream butter, and a good, not too lean cheese ; a large quantity of milk is worked up, 55,0001 b. for instance, in the week ending June 18th. The cream from the finest skimming, taken off after the milk has stood nine or ten hours, is used for sweet cream butter, 11b. of such butter requiring 35.41 b of milk; from the cream of subsequent skimming a small quantity of sour cream butter is prepand ; taking both kinds of butter to- gether, 3121 b. of milk are required for 11b. of butter. Never less than 0.5 per cent. of fat is left in the skimmed milk, this limit being strictly fixed in order that the cheese shall be fair in quality. To cool the milk as quickly as possible the tanks in which the milk vessels are to be set are first nearly filled with broken ice and a little water; the milk pails, of oval form and holding about 701 b. each, are then forced down into this thick ice-pap ; in forty-five minutes the milk falls from 86deg. to 68deg., and in thirty minutes more to 55deg. ; when skimmed the temperature of the milk is about 36deg. The cream is heated to about 52deg. preparatory to churning ; in the winter it is heated about 31eg. higher ; the same is done if the cows have been fed on old hay, or if there has been an unusually large propor- tion of beans and vetch in their rations. The churning occupies from twenty-seven to thirty minutes ; no water is added during this operation skimmed milk being used to rinse down the Bides of the churn; the butter comes in small pellets, like pin-heads, and the churning is stopped at this point; the butter is gathered in a strainer, and kneaded with the hands; salt is added at the rate of three-eighths of an ounce to the pound, and after more working with the hands the butter is made up into 51b. rolls and laid in an ice chest, where it remains an hour and a half and cools down to 52deg. again, when it is finally kneaded with the butter worker. Kneading at first with the hands is pre- ferred because, as it is claimed, the butter-milk is more completely worked out. The utmost cleanliness is main- tained throughout the factory, and scrupulously careful 'attention is required to the details of the management of the cream and buttes, under the immediate supervision of the skilled dairywoman who has the whole in charge. The product of the factory is in nearly all cases ranked as first- class by the Copenhagen exporters, whose judgment in the matter is held in extraordinary respect.

Gnowmo OLD.—It seems but a summer since we looked forward with eager hopes to coming years. And now we are looking sadly back. Not that the dream has passed, but that it has been of no more worth to those around us. As the glowing hopes and ambitions of early life pass away; as friend after friend departs, and the stronger ties which hold us here are broken, our lives seem but a bubble, glancing for a moment in the light, and then broken, and not a ripple on the stream. Forty years once seemed a long and weary pilgrimage to tread. It now seems but a step. And yet along the way are broken shrines where a thousand hopes have wasted into ashes; footprints sacred under their drift- ing duet ; green mounds, whose grass is fresh with the watering of tears; shadows, even, which we would not for- get. We will garner the sunshine of those years; and with chastened step and hopes push on towards the even- ing whose signal lights will soon be seen swinging where the waters are still and the storms never beat. FLOBILINE !—Fort TOTE TENTH AND BRICATH.—A few drops of he liquid " Floriline" sprinkled on a wet tooth brush produces a pleasant lather which thoroughly cleanses the teeth from all parasites or impurities, hardens the gums, prevents tartar, stops decay, gives to the teeth a peculiar pearly-whiteness, and a de- lightful fragrance to the breath. It removes all unpleasant odour arising from decayed teeth or tobacco smoke. The rragrant rloriline," being cornpcsed In part of honey and sweet herbs, is delicious to the taste, and the greatest toilet discovEr3 of the age. XI. One of the sections of the Land Bill of the Farmers' Alliance provides that where a tenant deteriorates a holding the landlord may apply to the Court at any time on or be- fore the determination of the tenancy, and the Court !shall assess the amount of damage, if any, done by the tenant, and order him to pay the amount thereof; and if such deterioration be persisted in by the tenant, the Court may order the tenant to give up possession of the holding to the landlord on such terms as the Court thinks fit. Everyone will agree with this, for if future legislation is to protect the tenant, it must also fully protect the landlord ; and having previously dealt with what ought to be done for the farmers in the way of some degree of Fixity of Tenure, Fair Rents, 1 full compensation for unexhausted and permanentlmprove- ments, freedom of cropping, and freedom of disposing to the best advantage of what they do grow, we now come to what the farmers might and ought to do for themselves, for "God helps those who help themselves." While it is a fact that the majority, probably the great majority, of the farms of England, are" under wrought, under cropped, and under capital led," owing partly to the conditions which surround their occupancy, the tenants themselves have it in their own power to improve matters by better farming, and when the laws having reference to the relations of Landlord and Tenant have been amended so to secure to the latter durable tenure, light rents, and ade- quate compensation for permanent improvements, there will be no reasonable excuse for the indifferent agriculture which is now much too common. Our English farmers, as a rule, have not sufficient capi- tal per acre. Mr. Mechi, in his work " How to Farm Pro- fitably," says :—"We all farm too much land, and so com- plain of want of capital. Experience teaches me that our cultivation is too shallow, • our manure toe little, and oar produce too small. No man ever ruined his root and green crops by filling the land to the depth of two feet with good manure. When I told my farming friends that Mr. Bagley, of Fulham, grew 70 tons of mangel per acre, and sold them at 20s. per ton to Mr. Rhodes, the cow keeper, there was a shout Of laughter, and something said about a ' crammer' but market gardeners, who cultivate four times as deeply '. and manure four times as heavily as ordinary farmers, loch : upon such a crop as nothing extraordinary. Our tillage is ' miserably shallow. . . . . I see before me," adds Mr. ' Meche "a man whe lost most of his money on 50 acres, but : now keeping the same etreenbt of stock upon 10 acres, he is 1 recovering himself and paying his way." In the seme book ' we have a specimen of whet an active and intelligent fare mer with ample capital does. Mr. John Hudson, of Castle ' Acre, Norfolk, told Mr. Mechi that during his long tenure 1 (25 to 30 years) of a farm of 1,200 acres, he had expended £70,000 in cake and £50,000 in artificial manures; and Mr. Mechi saw for himself that, in a favourable year, Mr. Hud- son had produced upon a 40 acre field of wheat, the amezing crop of 8i quarters-68 bushels per acre. The Marquis of Lansdowne said some time ago to the . farmers at Caine (when presiding at a lecture with the object of advancing scientific agriculture) things point in the direction of smaller estates for landholders, and smaller farms for farmers to meet American competition in meat, dairy produce, and corn. In stage language we may say, ''Tis well, my noble lord." Mr. Brodrick thinks that the establishment of Tenant Right, or the legal right to be reimbursed for his permanent improvements, will show the English farmer the advantage of spreading his capital over a smaller number of acres, if by so doing he can make it yield nearly the same rate of interest, besides reducing his rent and labour bill. Hence increased security of tenure will constantly operate to pro- mote the sub-division of very large holdings, except so far as it may attract new capital from business into farming, or encourage the development of joint stock agriculture on a grand scale. The process of subdivision, however, is likely to be very gradual. Like the landowner who measures his dignity by acreage rather than by income, the big farmer will at first be unwilling to ride over a smaller number of fields, or to superintend a smaller number of labourers. Moreover, farm buildings are not so eesily sub-divided as farms, and the many thousands of expensive steadings erected during the last thirty or forty years, will long con- tinue as a material guarantee for the policy of consolidation to which they owe their origin. Mr. Broderick goes on to show that it does not follow that the tenant of a medium- sized farm possesses less practical capacity or less capital in proportion to acreage than the farmer of a thousand acres and upwards. On the contrary, like his ancestors in Adam Smith's time, he is usually content to be his own overseer and foreman, knowing the value of the master's eye in all manual work, and will not be above occa- sionally putting his own hand to the plough. He may, perhaps be too liable to err on the side of penny wisdom, but he thus avoids the risk of sinking money in costly ex- periments and the breeding of prize animals. His wife is not too fine a lady to look after the fowl-yard or to superin- tend at least the making of butter and cheese. His farm buildings and fences may not be kept as neatly as they might be, and many things which offend the eye of a gentle- man farmer are tolerated on his land, but, at all events, he takes c ire to get money's worth for money, and is not ashamed to drive a hard bargain at the end of a market day. He does rot allow middlemen to run away with the lion's share of his legitimate profits by paying an exorbitant price for store cattle and selling fat beasts to a butcher for a sum far below the retail value of their meat. He keeps neither hunter nor dog-cart; if there is a piano in his parlour, ills a cheap one, and seldom used; his scale of household expen- diture is niggardly; and it is to be feared that his charit- able subscriptions come to very little in the course of the year. In short, he is a keen man of business, with the same turn for petty economies as a grocer or draper of equal income. Mr. Brodrick concludes that it is by no means im. probable that subdivision rather than consolidation of hold- ings may hereafter be dictated by the mutual interests of landlords and tenants. Nor will this chaege always in- volve any considerable outlay in buildings, for in many cases the homesteads of extinct farms remain in good repair, surrounded by yards and sheds, though now .tenanted by farm labourers. The Marquis of Lansdowne, at the meeting before referred to, further said :—Farmers must own themselves beaten, or use every scientific and practical means to promote produc- tion. Landowners and farmers must work together. Ile approved of the freedom of cropping, but the farmer should have scientific knowledge to use that freedom for the good of all. Certainly, if value is to be got either. out of the land or out of live stock, both capital and brains are re. quired—value must be firsteput in, and intelligent care and attention are necessary whether it be a 20 acre field or a hatch of chickens. Among many farmers, however, especi- ally of the old school, a contempt for and distrust of " book laming" has been prevalent, and they have eostinued on in their old "jog trot" style, working their farms on the principle of "role of thumb." That might be all well enough when they were protected by comparatively high prices and not subjected to the competition of cheap food from abroad, but in these days of rivalry in trade the old style of farming must be abandoned, and they mist bring to bear on their business (for farming ought to be considered a business) every improvement which scientific agriculta- riots have proved to be sound. They will find not only that "Knowledge is power," but that "Knowledge means money profit" too, and great credit is due to many country papers for the efforts they make to disseminate in their respective districts the latest scientific discoveries of practical and re- liable men, well known in agricultural matters. Every farmer ought to take and read a good country paper which devotes a portion of its space to agricultural topics, and in addition he would find it to pay if he took a purely agri- cultural paper like the Mark Lane Express, which teems with valuable information of all kinds for the farmer, while the series of prize essays published by that paper deserve the widest circulation. The cost of such a paper bears no comparison whatever with the monetary value of the know- ledge conveyed, often the result of the long and careful ex- perience of practical farmers. " Book-larning " or " theory " by itself is almost certain to fail. What is wanted is theor combined with practice, and if farmers would read more it would be to their own decided advantage. Take for instance the paper by Mr. Smetham, of Liver- pool, entitled "The economic use of artificial manures and foods," recently read at Lancaster on the occasion of the annual meeting of the Royal Manchester and Liverpool and North Lancashire Agricultural Society. Mr. Smetham, after showing clearly the sufficiency and advantage of various artificial manures, advised each farmer to arrive at a clear knowledge of the requirements of his own soil, and this obtained he would often find it more advantageous to mix the manures for himself, or at least to know exactly what elements he was placing in the land in the form of a mixed manure. He further said that the practical utility of a just conception of the composition and functions of manure would be readily acceded, and they would find no difficulties in applying the knowledge to any particular case. An important advantage to be derived f rom an intelligent understanding of what took place in the soil was found in the fact that with this knowledge they could often manure with the element most needed for a particular crop, as the stimulus thus given to the plants would enable them to ap- propriate a sufficient quantity of other elements, provided the land be in good condition. The practice of special manuring he believed was capable of much greater develop- ment, but it must be done intelligently,. Exactly, the ques- tion of artificial manures is one on which our farmers have much to learn, and the information will prove of very considerable money value to them, besides protecting them from the rubbish now often sold. Professor Tanner, in a recent lecture in the south of England, showed that every crop grown on the land necessarily made a demand on the soil for certain materials, which were built up in its structure and planted in its growth. It was Important to return to the soil some equivalent for that which was taken from it by exhaustion. It was his convic- tion that the future of farming was likely to be character- ised by greater thoroughness of cultivation than ever it had been in the past, and it would be found that in those in- stances in which the difficulties bad been less, were those cases in which there had been a thoroughness in the culti- vation of the land. He believed the day was fast approach- ing when farmers would not buy manures simply as manures, but they would acquaint themselves as to what materials they were using in them. So far, however, from the improvement hoped for by the Professor being immi- nent, it is too often the case that our farmers at present have not learned the best mode of treating their farmyard manure, which is left exposed to the weather, and washed by the rain, the value being thereby deteriorated, and the best part of it allowed to leak away and become lost, for it is anything but a rule for farmyards to be supplied with a tank for liquid manure. A want of management is also shown in the cultivation of the fie'ds th:mselves. They are often not finished. Odd

corners and wide headlands are not utilised, and wide hedge backs are wild with weeds. A really good farmer would not have a square yard wasted A want of care is often shown in the selection of seeds. Here there is no real economy in purchasing inferior seed, for the sake of a slight saving in price. It should be the best obtainable, though not necessarily show seed at a fancy price, and it should be of a kind suited to the soil and climate. _ _

The same remark applies to live stock. Take the breed- ing of horses for instance. The Mark Lane Express shows that there is an increasing demand for the best animals, and a decreasing demand for all others. With regard to draught horses, howeder, the money value of the beat and most suitable for town work is proportionately very much greater than that of second-rate animals, and consequently farmers are beginning to realise the very obvious fact that they may as well breed good ones when they are about it. The plan too often followed has been to breed from such mares only as were from some cause or other incapacitated from taking their full share of ordinary farm work, such animals being, generally speaking, unsound; and to use the nearest low-priced stallion, without any reference to sound- ness at all. If horses are fit for heavy town work at five years old, they will realise from £2O to £5O more money than they are worth at their best for farm work, and the extra expense of breeding such horses as these consists almost solely in an extra sovereign or two, and the loss of time in respect of mares in their prime. The information collected by the Mark Lane Express from all the great railway and carrying companies as to the kind of horse most in denl3nd is most valuable. - .

. Agin, as to cattle, sheep, and pigs. A farmer treed not go in for animals specially adapted for show purposes, but a well-bred animal takes no more food, in fact less, than an inferior animal, and is calculated to pay better, for in fatten- ing, as has been said, " the good animal eats less, grows faster, and when fat hat its meat in the most valuable parts." There is also much room for improvement in the manage- ment of live stock on a farm. The better they are protected and cared for, the less food they consume ; and the more suitable the food, the better they prosper. In France, whence we derive such a large quantity of our butter, the small farmers, with their limited holdings, cannot afford to turn their cows out into the pastures to trample and waste nearly as much as they eat No ; they must make the most of their small farms, and they either keep their cows in the stall, like some of our dairymen, or in comfortable yards, and cut the grass and cart it home. They thereby make the produce of a pasture field go further, and a greater number of cattle can be kept. The dung made in the yard is more 1 valuable, and if the cattle are for feeding purposes they lay on flesh faster. The pasture fields are rnanured and kept in good condition by tank liquid, and the yard manure, as be- fore observed, from being made and kept under cover, is more valuable. Will anyone deny that there la not much room for im- provement in England in this respect? If more cattle were thus kept, should we not have a greater home production of beef, milk, butter, and cheese, and less imported from abroad? The raising of fat stock is likely to be a permanently re- liable and remunerative occupation. On inferior animals good food is almost wasted, while on better bred stock the outlay is amply repaid, and, as the object should be to get ' the cattle ready for the butcher in the least possible time, ' the questions of the best and most suitable stock and the right kind of food are all-important. Here, again, many of : our farmers could obtain much valuable information from ' agricultural papers as to the relative values of linseed cake, : cotton cake, maize, rice meal, palm nut meal and cake, and . cocoa nut cake, malt, dec., and the. amount and manner ot , their supply to the cattle; and the information so gained : would not only save money but make money.

A lady once said to Mr. 'Wesley," Suppose you knew that you were to die at twelve o'clock to-morrow night, how would you spend the intervening time ?" "How, madam?" was the reply; "why, just as I intend to spend it now. I should preach this evening at Gloucester and again at five o'cloc'a to-morrow morning. After that I should ride to Tewkesbury, preach in the afternoon, and meet the Societies in the evening. I should then repair to friend Martin's house, who expects to entertain me; converse and pray with the family as usual; retire to my room at ten o'clock ; com- mend myself to my Heavenly Father; lie down to rest and wake up in glory.' A RUSSIAN DETECTIVE.—A couple of years ago there was published at Geneva a volume of memoirs by a Russian spy, who took the name of Nicholas Zaroubolf. He acknoat- 'edged in his preface that this was not his real name, and that he was a fugitive, having been unfortunate in the management of a delicate mission entrusted to him abroad, which made him fearful of returning to Russia. What this misdon was he does not state; but from internal evidence in his writings it is easy to see that he did hold the confi- dential position which he alleges, and was at one time much trusted by the Russian Court. He accompanied the late Czar to London, when his Majesty visited England after the Duke of Edinburgh's marriage in 1874, and he describes the extraordinary precautions taken by the Home Secretary and Colonel Henderson to protect the Czar against assassi- nation. Zarouboff did not travel as a police agent. He was supposed to be a gentleman of the suite, and accompanied the Emperor everywhere, even to the banquet in St. George's Hall, Windsor. At the Guildhall, when the freedom of the city was presented to the Czar, Zarouboff had a great fright. He was standing close tp the Emperor when he noticed among the newspaper reporters a man whom he knew to be a Poliah refugee. He stroked his left ear, whichlwas a sign to the chief of the Russian detectives present to approach him, and in a few words he informed this official of his suspicion. The Russian slipped away and communicated with his English colleagues, who quickly got round the Pole. This man, all unconscious of the attention bestowed upon him, was quietly taking notes for a German paper. Presently he put his hand into a pocket and drew out a long leather tube. Before he could open it a .jerk of his elbow caused it to fall out of his hand, and the London de- tective who picked it up pulled off the lid. It proved to be a common case for holding pens and pencils. The Pole saw, however, that be was under surveillance, and, growing very red, said he would not stay to be insulted. No oppo- sition was made to his exit, but a detective followed him out of the Guildhall and offered him a word of friendly re- monstrance against showing himself in the Czar's way. The Pole answered bitterly that he had more to fear from the Czar than the Czar from him; and he went off, after giving his card and convincing the emissary from Scotland Yard that he was an honourable man who had been wrongly suspected.—Cornhill Magazine. £l.O TO £5). —TOBACCONISTS COMMENCING.—A.PamphIet, How to Open a Shop fmm LW. post free.—Address, H. The outbreak of typhoid fever in Oldham is spreading.

Two Exeter servant girls, after visiting Exmouth, have mysteriously disappeared. A London contemporary announces on authority that the Princess Louise fully intends to return to Canada in the Spring. At Cleckheaton on Saturday, Joseph Firth, known as "Steeple Jack," fell from the lofty chimney of a mill, and was killed instantaneously.

• _ An attempt was made on Sunday mornirg to break into the Battle branch of the Lewes Old Bank, but the burglars being disturbed, nothing wasstolen. The Daily Telegraph says the report is authoritively con- tradicted that the Hon. Evelyn Ashley, M.P., intends to re-

sign the secretaryship of the Board of Trade. About noon on Sunday, jewellery to the value of between £30,000 and £40,000 was stolen from the mansion of Lord Arthur Hill-Trevor, near Chirk. The valet and ikincipal housemaid are in custody on suspicion. No clue to the missing property has been obtained. On Monday night the Salvation Army at Reading cele- brated the opening of their new barracks, a substantial structure capable of holding 2000, persons, which they have just erected in one of the poorest and most densely-populated districts of the town.

THE MASSACRE OE 200 YOUNG GIRLS—The Daily News learns by the last mail from the Gold Coast that the in- telligence of the massacre of 200 young girls by the King of Lhante9 has been Confirmed by the report of a native of that country who had come down to the coast. Mr. Leveson7Gower, addressing his constituents at Bodmin, on Monday, said no bubble had ever burst as the bubble of Protection had. He advocated the abolition of the law of distress, and expressed a hope that the Government would introduce a good measure of county goveinment embodying substantially the programme of the Farmer's Alliance. Mr. Bradlaugh, M.P., delivered a lecture on Sunday, at the 11 of Science, on our national expenditure and its increase during the present reign. Ile said that when he took his seat in the House he should call attention to the expenditure incurred for the royal family, the army, navy, and civil forces. Steps are being taken by the heads of the Wesleyan Methodist body for the erection of an orphanage, near Bir- mingham. When completed the orphanage will accomodate 300 children, and a chapel will also be provided to afford convenience for 000 worshippers. The whole scheme is to cost £19,000. A silver cradle was on Tuesday presented to Mrs. William Laird, Mayoress of Birkenhead, by the members of the town council and other friends, that lady having given birth to a daughter during the mayoralty of her husband. A me- mento of the happy event was also presented to each one of his worship's six children. DEATII FROM OVERJOY.—A MOST PAINFUL INCIDENT.— A most painful occurrence was witnessed on Saturday at Upper Gornal, Sedgley, Staffordshire. A woman, named Ann Blackham, was so overjoyed at the return home of her son, whom she had not seen for years, that she went to ' meet him, and, after giving him a very happy greeting, fell dead at his feet. THE OPENING OF PARLIAMENT.—On cut that in order to give greater eclat to the proposals which the Government have in contemplation, the Queen has already been asked to open Parliament in person. Those who know, remarks the Wor/d, say that as matrimonial provision will be asked for Prince Leopold and his bride, the Queen may personally consent to express her gratification at the approaching union of her favourite son. Sir Stafford Northcote, writing to a correspondent at Bristol en the subject of "Fair Trade," says that as he an- ticipates full discussion of the question in the course of next session he "thinks it well to wait for that opportunity of entering into its merits." It is to be understood, therefore, that there are" merits "in the arguments of the "Fair-traders." It is tantalising of Sir S. Northcote to putoff their disclosure for several months. At the Bradford Police Court, on Tuesday, John Tobin, labourer, was again brought up on a charge of treason-felony. Mr. Pollard, who prosecuted for the Treasury, said it had caused the authorities in London a good deal of anxiety as to how best to deal with the prisoner. They thought that the best course was to place the evidence before the Court, and leave it to the discretion of the magistrates to commit the prisoner to trial for treason-felony, or such charge as they thought necessary. The prisoner was further remanded. That the revolver is becoming an indispensable part of a burglar's equipment is shown by cases which have occurred at Croydon and Northampton. In the former case a county police officer encountered a burglar who fired three shots at him, two of which pierced his clothing. The officer was unable to capture the assailant. In the latter case a couple of burglars who were " disturbed " by the police showed fight. One of the officers was stunned with a blow from a heavy weapon, and the other was menaced with a pistol at his head. One of the burglars, WS arrested and was on Monday remanded by the Croydon magistrates.

ROTITLEDGR CHRISTMAS NUMBER (London: Geo. Rout- ledge and Sons) is one of the best Christmas annuals for children that we have seen this year as yet. Its severa stories are delightfully written, whilst the eight chief illusit trations are beautifully produced in colours, making

altogether a very attractive and interesting publication-fo the little ones. On the cover is an appropriate and season able illustration showing the snow, the robin redbreasts, the church tower, and around the hearth numbers of pairs of tiny shoes waiting for Santa Claus' visit. MYRA'S JOURNAL (London: Gouband and Sons, 39, Bed- ford-street, Covent Garden).—The Christmas double number of this popular monthly is certainly a surprising shilling's woith. In addition to the usual contents this number is replete with a large fund of information specially interesting to the fair sex, including articles on " employment for women," marriage settlements and laws for the protection of married women, menus for 1882, &c. The number is also accompanied with a splendid chromo-lithographic picture entitled "A woodland beauty," printed in colours. THE WORTHIES OF THE WORLD (Ward, Lock, and Co., Salisbury-square).—Part 13 of this excellent and popular work contains short well written biographies of Her Majesty the Queen, Joan of Arc, Queen Elizabeth, and Charlotte Bronte. These very interesting sketches of notable women appropriately make up the concluding part of this volume. The publishers make the gratifying announcement that in consequence of the very favourable reception accorded to this series they purpose issuing a second series in the course of the coming year. THIRTEEN AT DrsniEn (London: Griffith and Ferran; Bristol : J. W. Arrowsmith).—Under this title we have a new annual by a number of authors some of whom are well known. We congratulate Mr. Arrowsmith and his friends on having produced a work which contains a very pleasant mixture of tales, sketches, poetry, and music, which we have no doubt will have a large sale, and which certainly deserves to have a place amongst the permanent productions that usually appear at this season of the year. Some of the tales are certainly well written, and are very interesting, whilst the illustrations are of a high order. THE SCREW or DEATH (London: Gant and Co., Turn- mill-street). Notwithstanding the somewhat ghastly title given to this annual we ventured to peruse its contents, and found it to be an interesting story of the usual Christmas character. It is full of love and adventure, and is a well sustained and powerfully written story, as we might have expected, seeing that it comes from the pen of Mr. Francil- len, a practised and well known writer. The story is a weird one, and the plot is well laid, so that those who are fond of the mysterious will read the tale with thrilling interest to the end. The tale is said to be founded on facts, and is alleged to be a chronicle of a series of remarkable events which befell a number of people. The illustrations are very attractive. LETT'S POPULAR ATLAS, Part 23.—Those of our readers interested in geography (and who in this great mercantile country should not be ?) who are not already taking in this excellent work, should commence with Part 21, which is now giving large scale maps of Europe with the capital cities. As the greatest carrying, importing and exporting nation of the world, it is only natural that we should be concerned in knowing in what our various interests abroad consist, and in this new series we can see clearly and fully. Take the little country of Portugal for instance; we note that one of its staple articles of export is cork, both un- manufactured and manufactured; we note that for the last five years the trade has gone down, and that the bulk of the raw material comes from the country in question, while IFrance takes the lead in the manufactured article. We im- port more and more annually of oxen and bulls, copper re- gulus (whatever that may be), oranges and lemons, onions (evidently the so-called Spanish, .although our chief market for them appears to be Holland), pyrites of iron or copper, and wool, whilst in quicksilver and wine the:trade appears to be falling off. But, perhaps, the leading feature of these large scale maps (being mostly, the same as that of the beauti- ful geological map of England in the first series) is the in- troduction of a red cross and circle to indicate the towns where the British Government possesses a consul or vice- consul. Of the general geographical features we can but repeat that th seem to be clear and well printed as usual and the additioney of the lighthouses ought to increase the value considerably. The work is one of the most interesting we have seen and is well worthy of the title "Popular.'.

div.p: THE EXAMINER, SAT URDAY DECEMBER 10, 1881.

WA.IIIIIITGTON VA KLIDIENTARY "DE B ATI NG- SOCIETY. The future prospects of the society again engaged the attention of the members o_n Monday night. The Liberal binches were moderately Well filled, but there were only one or two Conservative members present. The strangers who assembled appeared to listen to the discussion with great interest. Dr. Huson-More (the Speaker) presided. lie said he' had received a letter from Mr, W. J. Burgess, the leader of the Opposition, in which he thanked him on his own behalf and on that of the Conservative ilembers generally, for the very fair and impartial manner in which he had presided over the debates of the society. The following resolution was enclosed That the letter of Dr. Mason- More has been duly corsidered, and•the Conservatives have decided that their reasons for withdrawing from the society still retain their force, and have rather been intensified than otherwise by the resolution passed on Monday, November 21st, and by language used by the Premier; and are there- fore unable to comply with the suggestion made that a con- ference ef the leaders of the party should be held."—Mr. Macau; (Conservative) considered that the members who had seceded could not have a very high sense of duty to go away in the childish manner in which they had done. (Hear, hear.) If they did not consider it right for the right hon. member for Northampton to make the remark he did it was ruled to be strictly parliamentary, and it would have been better to have made a concession than to secede from the house. (Hear, hear.) He wished to ask the Premier to take into consideration the few members who were on his side of the house, as, although they were few, they constituted a small party—about as large as the fourth party in the Honseof Commons. (Laughter.) He thanked the Premier. and the Liberal party generally for the gentlemanly and courteous manner in which they had been treated during the last few weeks, and he hoped • they' would allow the few Conservative members to remodel themselves as party. (Applause.) He should not like the society to break down and the Conservatives were not so broken down in the town but that there were still a few men who would come forward. (Applause.)—Mr. Percy thought the matter would blow over, and be was wishful as one anxious for the welfare of the society, that nothing should be said that Vonld aggravate things more than they were.. (Hear, hear.) He hoped Mr. Machin's suggestion would be adopted.-e-The Chairman said that after the com- munication be had received, it appeared that nothing more could be done in that matter.—Mr. Jacobsen moved that the subscription of the society be reduced to a shilling, and that placards be posted inviting workingmen to join the society. If this was done be thought they would have as large a party as ever they had.—Mr. Witham said if they could in- duce real workingmen to enter they would do some good in the town. If they reduced the fee he was afraid they would again give offence to the Tories by making it appear a money matter.—The Rev. R. Pitcher, B. A., said be felt so thoroughly contemptuous of the utter falseness underlying the whole of the Opposition's proceedings—(hear' hear,)— and utterances that he would not trust himself to speak further upon it, and pass it over with the. disdain he felt. (Hear, bear.) The practical difficulty lay in the fact that they had had great expense not only in taking that large hall, but also in printing, in regard to which he believed they had entered into obligations until the end of December. Consequently he feared that the funds of the society would not bear the grain of continuing—certainly in that place,— and he thought it would be better if a council meeting was called to prepare a statement of accounts and adjourn that meeting until Monday night. They would then see what was the real state of affairs.—Mr. Chapman seconded the re- solutien.—Mr. Winskill read a letter he had received from Mr. George Woods, who stated that he went to the Conserva- tive meeting on Saturday night, with the intention of en- deavouring to heal the dissension between the two parties, but he was shown a report of the Prime Minister's speech delivered on the 21st ultimo, when he stated " it I was tone in the opposite camp to tell a lie •, it was tone to I get up in a gentlemanly way next night and apologise, as If an apology could wipe out a fraudulent transaction." (Hear, hear.) Mr. Woods considered it ungentlemanl7 and ungenerous to refer to his apology in that way. If this was the conduct of those who knew what good manners were, what were they to expect to be the conduct of those who did not ?—Mr. Winskill thought the Prime Minister's love of punning had sometimes given o ' ffence and asked the mem- bers to remember they all had sensitive feelings.—The Rev. R. Pitcher begged to say that what he said the other night was said not as a pun but in sober seriousness. (Hear, bear.) The phrase " tone" was not of his invention. (Hear, hear.) Again and again had the Conservatives flung at their heads that they wanted tone,wnd in the fraudulent—he could use no other word—letter which they published in the "neutral" organ before the Speaker could possibly have seen the I original, the very phrase was used. .(Hear, hear.) Very I well, he appealed to the whole House and asked was not the hon. member for Montrose told at the time that it was not as he said—(hear, hear)—and that he was mistaken? Did not he and his party use .that mistake .to rouse the passions of his own side, and when this so-called apology was made had not the mistake done its deadly work? Then with what face could Mr. Woods turn round and say that the reason was be (Mr. Pitcher) spoke the plain truth about his conduct? He said again that no .apology could wipe out the fraudulency of such a transaction.. (Hear, hear.) The gentlemen who could publish in a paper a formal document, and who had been guilty of mistakes persevered in so long as they could be useful to their party in raising angry pas- sion, and still presumed that they had an amount of tone and polish which was not possessed on the Liberal side of the House, those gentlemen put themselves out of court. He (Mr. Filcher) did once or twice make a pun on the hon. gentlemen opposite, and once or twice a joke against them. • Unfortunately some of his jokes had given offence; but very often he had recourse to a joke to ward off the butcherly attacks on the, other side because he could not weild —or rather would not descend —to weild the same weapons as those with which they assaulted them. (Applause.) For instance, the 'hon. member for Eye had compared them to butchers. ("Joke.") That was a joke. (Laughter.) The bitter retort was on his lips to "you, remnant of the butchers of Peter Loo" but instead of that he turned it off with a joke. And therefore for them now to come-at the last moment and make him the third scapegoat (laughter) showed, indeed, that they were hard up for a reason. His conduct ef the business in that house, as leader, was open to them at any time they had been welcome to impugn that conduct; and he challenged anyone to bring it to the testing of the fact. He had striven to conduct the_business of the house with good feeling—(hear' bear)—and at any time if he had parried attacks by a joke it had been that he might deprive the re- tort of the bitterness it otherwise would have. (Hear, bear.) But when gentlemen opposite mistook his forbearance for weakness, then he showed them what he would do, and he skinned them. (Applause.)—The resolution was then carried.—The orders of the day were then proceeded with, and the member for Boston moved " That it is desirable to give legislative effect to the just and reasonable principles in the Local Option resolution, passed in June, 1880, by con- ferricg upon local communities the power to protect them- selves from the operations of the liquor traffic."--The member for Evesham seconded the motion, which, alter a brief discussion, was declared carried, and he house ad- journed.

PRESCOT LOCAL BOARD. The monthly nieeling of this board was held on Wednes- day, Mr. Castle Spencely presiding. There were also pre- sent Messrs. H. Fogg, J. Wycherley, E. Beesley, T. S. Prts- ton, S. Bennett, and A. T. Galloway; with Mr. Cross (clerk) and Mr. W. Goldsworth (surveyor).

GENERAL PI7RPOSES COMMITTEE. At a meeting of this committee on Monday, the Assistant- Surveyor reported that the works for the bupply of water to houses in Hill-street and Stone-street had almost been completed.—Ordered that the necessary proceedings be taken to take down the dangerous shed in the Market-place. —A letter was read from Mr. Banks complaining of the deposit by others of rubbish on the intended new road on land of King's College at the junction of West-street and the Liverpool-road.—A plan was submitted on behalf of Mr. Wm. Evans, brewer, "'ascot, for the erection of a shed on the side of the late Mr. Bradshaw's house, and approved of, with a recommendation that a give-and-take line should be agreed on, with a view to improve both the highway and his property—Ordered that an exhaustive report of the cases of the abatement of, and the existence of, nuisances arising from large middens throughout the town be pre- pared.—The Surveyor reported that in consequence of the decrease of the scarlet fever cases. and these being of a less virulent character, the Medical Officer had, on last Wednes- day, dispensed with the nurse's services, and the hospital.— Ordered that an inventory of the articles purchased be made, and the goods put into store for use on any similar future occaion.—The minutes were passed.

FINANCE COMMITTEE. At a meeting; of this committee, Mr. C. Spreely presid- ing, it was resolved that application be made to the Locil Government Board for the remission of the sums of £3 30. and £liss. disallowed by the auditor.—The minutes were confirmed.

WARRINGTON POLICE COURT. MONDAY.—Bcfore the Mayor and Major Cartwright. A NARROW ESCAPE.—A youth named William Allen was charged with furiously driving down Buttermarket-street, endangering the lives of the foot passengers.—P.C. Neill said he saw the prisoner driving a butcher's conveyance at a furious rate down Buttermarket-street on Saturday, the 26th ult. When opposite Mr. Wood's shop the horse's foot struck a boy, who was crossing, and threw him against the kerbstone. "It was a miracle the bay was not killed."— Defendant was fined lOs and 5s MIS. DANGEROUS SHOOTING.—A boy named Peter Ecicersley was charged with throwing glass balls from a catapult, to the danger of passougers.—Defendant was seen by P.C. 14 sending heavy glass balls from a catapult in Marsh-house- lane on the 29th ult.—Defendant, who stated he was shoot- ing at birds, was fined 2s Gd. THE THEFT OF SHIRTS.—Joseph Corcoran, forgeman, and Thomas McHugh were brought up on remand charged with stealing three mixture woollen shirts, of the value of 7s ed, the property of Thomas Dale, draper, Bridge-street.—Priso- ners were committed to the sessions for trial. "No DEEDS, No MARRYING :" FORTUNE HUNTING. John Atherton was charged on a warrant with having, on the 3rd November, stolen a hair-seated sofa, an oblong table, two pairs of iron bedsteads, and other furniture, of the value of £2O, the property of Ellen Dixon.— Mr. Worsley (Ridgway and Worsley) prosecuted, and Mr. George Moore defended.—The prosecutrix, it apppeared, is a widow with two children, living at Haydock, and in August last she made the acquaintance of the prisoner, a collier working at the Lea Coalpit, Haydock. They agreed to be married, and Mrs. Dixon allowed the prisoner to re- move a portion of her furniture from her father's house where she lived, to a house at Black-brook, which was taken in her name. Subsequently the furniture was again removed to the house of the prisoner's brother in Knutsford-road, Latchford, and towards the end of October the prosecutrix paid him a visit there. During the 10 days'she stayed they lived as man and wife, and the banns were read at St. James' Church. At the end of that time, however, the prosecutrix learned that the prisoner had systematically deceived other women, and on the morning the wedding should have taken place she went home. Immediately after- wards the prisoner sold the furniture, stated to be worth £27 103. for £9 10s. to a broker, and a warrant was conse- quently issued for his apprehension. Prosecutrix is pos- sessed of some property, and the prisoner had wished to have his name put on the deeds which were kept by her father but she had replied that neither him nor any man should do that. When apprehended by P.C. Bowen, pri- soner said " We ought to have been married at Wigan, but I told her if there was no deeds there was no wedding." For the defence it was given in evidence that the prisoner and prosecutrix had stated their intention of going to America and that the latter had given prisoner authority to sell the furniture. On one occasion whilst sitting on his knee, it was stated that she said, referring to her father's opposition, " Ne'er mind, old lad, I'll hey' thee. If I hey' to sell my shift off my back I'll hey' thee."—The Bench re- manded the case on account of insufficiency of evidence, admitting the prisoner to bail, himself in £4O and two sureties in £2O each. TUESDAY.—Before Major Cartsvright and Councillor Monks. A FAMILY DESERTER PultisnEn.—John Pennington, a forge -labourer, was charged with having, on the 24th November, run away from the borough, leaving his wife and children chargeable to the common fund of the Union.—Mr. Harbourne said the prisoner's wife applied to him for relief on the 23rd ult., and he visited the house, which was in Berry's Court, Dallatn-ladt. He found the woman and her three children in a most destitute condition. In six weeks she had only received from the prisoner—who had gone to work at Wigan—the sum of ss. ed. The family were now in the Workhouse.—Prisoner was committed to gaol for a month. WEDNESDAY.—Before Councillor Fairclougb, and Alderman Chandley. THREATENING HIS MOTHER.—A young man named John Barlow was brought up, on remand, charged with using malicious threats towards his mother, Margaret Bulow, whereby she was afraid he would do her some bodily harm.—Prisoner was hound over to keep the peace for six mouths. THE Boy WHO WANTED TO EMIGRATE—John Henry Kearney, a boy, who was charged with robbing his mother, under circumstances previously detailed in the Examiner, again appeared before the Bench.-The mother said since he was last before the magistrates the lad had done very well ; he had been a very good lad.—P.C. Bowen said the lad was now working, and he was let off with a fine of 10s. and costs. Turns:a-v.—Before Alderman Webster and Councillor Milner. " TODDLE " SENT TO GAOL—Thomas Hart,better known as "Toddle," was charged with stealing 3s. 3d. from .the house of Elizabeth Lee, in Stamford-street. The prosecutor, on the previous day, was absent from home for about ten minutes, leaving in the house four small children. When she returned 3s. 3d., which had been on the mantle shelf, was not to be found. Her eldest daughter Annie, 7 years of age, told her "'Toddle ' Hart came in and wanted some money." Subsequently, the priemer offered to ieturn the money, and he was apprehended.—ln redly to the charge of Constable 14, he slid "You are a liar. lhat woman gave it to me." He now stated that he had pawhed his boots for the money, and denied the theft.—He was sentenced to three months' imprisonment,—Prisoner was then further charged with doing damage to the amount of 3s. al. in the police cell, and he was committed for an additional seven days.
NEWTON AND F,ARLESTOWN.
NEWTON IMPROVEMENT COMMISSIONERS.

_ The monthly meeting of this Board was held at the Town Hall, Newton-le-Willows, on Monday. In the absence of the chairman, Colonel McCorquodale presided, and there were also present Messrs. Wood, Emmett, Pardey, Fair- dough, Gillespie, Forster, J. E. Worsley (law clerk), and It. Brierley (surveyor). VOTES or CONDOLENCE.

The CHAIRMAN 1:e-teitrIci to the two deaths that had taken place since the last meeting, and could not but say that it appeared very sad indeed to him, as it would to them, the changes that had taken place by death in the last three months. Since the September meeting the Board had lost three commissioners—three very active ones. At the last meeting they alluded with very great regret and sorrow to the death of Mr, Birley, one of the comusissionerz since dead was present a month ago and took part in the remarks made concerning the death of that commissioner. He also took an active part in ths discussion at the meeting that day and be was sure they would feel Mr. Winstanley's loss very much indeed. He was a very active member, and was pos- sessed of a great deal of knowedge respecting the matters that came under the Board's observation. Mr. Pennington also took a very active part in the business of the Board, particularly as chairman of the Road Committee, and he (the chairman) was sure the Board would also miss him very much. He therefore proposed the following resolution : "'That the Commissioners desire to record their sense of the loss this Board has sustained by the deaths of the late Mr. Winstanlev and Mr. Pennington, who have for several years been most useful commissioners, and that the Commissioners desire to express to the families of the late Mr.Winstanley and Mr. Pennington the sympathy:of the Commissioners with them under their present bereavement; and that copies of this reso- lution under the common seal of the Board be forwarded by the Law Clerk to Miss. Winstanley and Mrs. Pennington." The Chairman, as an old commissioner, remarked that very few commissioners had died in harness. The resolution was seconded and agreed to.
THE LATE MR. IHRLEY.
A letter was read from Mrs. Birley, acknowledging the vote of condolence forwarded to her by the Board.
TEE VACANCIES ON THE BOARD.

Mr. EMMETT proposed the appointment of Mr. Benjamin Walker as a member of the Board in the place of the late Mr. Pennington. Mr. PennEy moved, and Mr. Ekinctounn seconded the appointment of Mr. Thomas Stone,to fill the vacancy caused .by the death of Mr. Winstanley. Mr. WOOD then proposed, and Mr. GILLESPIE seconded the election of Mr. Benjamin Glover in the place of Mr. Pennington. As 3ir. Ernmett's proposition was not seconded, the two latter propositions were put and carried unanimously. THE HOUSE-TO-HOUSE VISITATION.

A meeting of the Highway, Public Works, and Sanitary Committee was held on the 21st ult. Dr. Watkins attended to confer with the committee upon the report of the house- to-house visitation as to the extent Of scarlet fever and measles in the district. The report of the disinfector showed the number of cases reduced, and the Medical Officer stated that in his opinion the infection would die out during the , Christmas holidays, if the school managers could be induced to give a month's holiday. It was resolved to invite the school managers of the district to a conference with the com- mittee on sth December, to extend the holidays hem two to four weeks. It was ordered that £5 be paid to Messrs. J. Ball and J. Caldwell for .their house-to-house inspection and report upon the epidemic prevailing in the district. The adoption of the main roads in the district by the county authorities was again considered. The Law Clerk advised that the application be renewed. It was decided that the Law Clerk and Mr. Brierley wait on the committee at Preston if necessary, and adopt such steps as would secure their contributing to the maintenance of the main roads in the district. Mr. Brier- ley reported that he had issued the necessary notices for the making of Suez-street, Alma-street, and Grant-street. Ile also reported that several nuisances existed after due notice had been given to the offenders. It was ordered that legal proceedings be taken, and that it be an instruction to Mr. Brierley to take legal proceedings against all offenders of the committee's bye-laws without the necessity of a special resolution of the committee.

The minutes were adopted, with the exception of the one referring to legal proceedings being taken by Mr. Brierley, which was referred back. THE SCHOOLS TO BE CLOSED. A conference of the school managers was held shortly before the meeting of the Board, and it was resolved "that it is expedient on the report of the medical officer of health to close the schools of the district (both day and Sunday) for three weeks, from the 16th inst."

div.head: REGISTRAR'S_ REPORT.
div.p: REGISTRAR'S_ REPORT.

The Rcgistrar's report for November showed 20 births compared with 28 in the corresponding month of last year. Deaths, 15 against 11 last year; death-rate per thousand, 2804, corresponding month last year 2203. Eleven deaths were those of children under five years of age. Only two deaths had occurred from scarlet fever.

div.head: DISCONTINUANCE OF THE HOSPITAL.
div.p: DISCONTINUANCE OF THE HOSPITAL.

In accordance with notice of motion, Mr. Fogg moved that the tenancy of Cherley-house as a fever hospital be given up, and that the services of the nurse be dispensed with.—This was seconded by Mr. Wycherley and carfied.— The Medical Officer reported that the sebre ep:demic of searlet fever Nv hfa bad raged so fiercely for a short time in the town, had again left. There were only two cases left as far as he knew and those were of the mildest type. The fever hospital had been closed and the services of the nurse dispensed with. He thought they were indebted to the nurse and the nuisance inspector for their very effectual help in stamping out the disease. During the seven weeks the nurse was engaged she attended 101 cases in 48 different houses, and paid 349 visits. There were a. few cases of whooping cough in the town, but they did not seem to be of a very severe form. „ It was resolved that ral4EgwereßrAarl district rate of Is. 114. in the pound he laid to carry the board over till the 25th March nest, but that no portion of the rate should be col- lected till as =eat., of the old rate were got in.
