div.head: SCHOOL ATTENDANCE COMMITTEE.
div.p: SCHOOL ATTENDANCE COMMITTEE.

At a meeting of the School Attendance Committee, on the 21st ult., a letter was read from Mr. John W. Watkins, bon. sec. of St. Peter's district school, transmitting the following resolution on the question of half-time scholars, passed at a special meeting of the committee of managers:—" That the fees for half-timers at St. Peter's district school be Bd. per week, the moiety of which will be returned to each scholar obtaining a grant in the standards." It was ordered that the boy, Wm. Pullen, be again presented to the school with the ordinary weekly school fees, with a view to stating a case to the Education Department, if refused admission. The minutes were adopted, on the motion of Mr. FORSTER, Secouded by Mr. FARDEY.
FINANCE.
The Finance Committee—U.te-t.-Mi the 21st u/t., when ac- counts amounting to £458 were examined and cheques signed for payment.
THEFT OF AN EARL'S BODY IN-
ABERDEENSHIRE.

A painful discovery has been made at Dnnecht, near Aberdeen, the seat of the Earl of Cr.awford and Balcarres. It has been found that the body of the late Earl had been stolen from the private mortuary attached to the family chapel. The deceased nobleman died in Italy. The crime is sup- posed to have been committed acme considerable time ago. Three coffins were broken open. In the absence of any other probable motive it is supposed that the body has been carried away by Florentines who planned the villany at the time of the Earl's death, and that the object is to gain a substantial sum by way of ransom. An anonymous letter has been received in Aberdeen from Glasgow, in which the writer purports to give an account of the robbery of the Earl of Crawford's body by confederates. He expresses his sorrow that he had anything to do with the matter, seeing that the body is not put back, as was promised by those concerned. He states that he lived for one year in Aberdeen. He lodged with a friend, a joiner, who has also left the the town. One night, about May 6tlior Bth, while working with his friend, two gentlemen called to see the latter. As there was only a light in one corner of the room, the writer could not see their faces. They engaged in con- versation, which he could not hear. After the visitors had ' gone his friend asked him if ke would assist him in a big job. He agreed, but was rather stirtled when told it was to carry away the body of the Earl of Crawford. The reward, however, was large. Eight days later, when the two gentle- men called again, they said they were medical men, and would put back the body when done with it. On the Friday night following he and his friend went out to meet the gentlemen; but they did not come. Next night, however, they met, and drove in a dog cart some distance. The horse was unharnessed, and the writer was left to mind it, while the others went away. They were some hours absent, and he fell asleep. It was past midnight, and on their return he was awakened by their conversation. His friend and another man were carrying a long bundle, and, on being asked, they said it was the Earl's body. They drove back as far as the entrance to the town, where he and his friend alighted, it being then after three in the morning. The writer says the gentlemen stated that they only wanted the body for a few days, in order to find out the process of embalming.

div.head: WIN SFORD.
div.p: WIN SFORD.
A new juvenile society under the title of the Winsford Dialogue Society, began a series of entertainments on Friday last in the Weaver Schools, in recitations and music. They were well patronised.

THE Acsnxtri WursForm—The annual concert and prize day at tbe Academy, Winsford, will be held on Tues- day next, when the principals. Mr. and Mrs. Buckley will be pleased to see old and present pupils to tea at four,and con.- cert at half-past six p.m. The next term will begin January 17th, 1882.

SALT TRADE, WtersronD.—The salt trade is now in reality beginning to feel the effects of the recent tempest. We have no ships left to carry our salt since the havoc made amongst the Norwegian, German, and other wooden fleets daring the last two months, has deprived the salt trade almost entirely of the means of transport The extraordinary falling off in demand is testified by subjoined export list, and accounted for as above. Prices- are, therefore, naturally to a great extent nominal, and altogether very irregular. Indeed it is years since there has been such a falling off as during the past November; not in the make of salt, but in its export, though it cannot fail to affect its manufacture. If we except the years 1876 and 1877, when the total export n Nbvember fell to 2,360 tons below the present month, we have no instances so low within the decade. The falling off is marked in every quarter, sho sing that the storms have had a baneful effect in every direction. To the States we sent in November 18,932 tons, against 23,527 last year ; to British North America 959, against 4,140; to the West Indies and South America 1,751, against 1,168; to A'rica 1,160, against 3,086; while Calcutta has taken 23 002, against 9,557 in November last, which is the only large instance of increase. Rangoon has taken 1,100, against 6,116; and the Australian Colonies 3,571 tone, a decrease on the previous November of 4,204 tons. Prussia took this year 1,372, as against 3,363 last year; while to Russia have gone 1904, as compared with 740 of previous year. Other Baltic ports have received about the same this year as last, but France and the Mediterranean have fallen from 705 to 116 this year. Newcastle has risen from 348 tons last year to 457 this November, but the rest of England has nothing against 490 of November, 1880. Scotland has 1,024, against • 1,243 of previous November; and Ireland 290, against nothing in 1880. Holland has risen from last year's 1,317 to 2,621; but Belgium has fallen to 2,629 from 3,498. The total exports from Liverpool have fallen from 62,517 in November, 1880, to 56,310 last month; and Runcorn and Weston docks from 15,131 to 9,740; or the total from the Mersey exported in November has fallen from 77,648 to 6.6,050 in this year, doubtless from the causes named.

div.head: MR. p. W. LATHAM ON AGRICULTURAL REFORM.
div.p: MR. p. W. LATHAM ON AGRICUL- TURAL REFORM.

At a large meetiog of tenant farmers at Chester, on Saturday, an address on the programme of the Farmers' Alliance was delivered by Mr. Barclay, M.P. for Forfar'. shire. Mr. G. W. Latham; the Liberal candidate for Mid-Cheshire, subsequently rose to move .a resolution affirming the principles of the Tenant Farmers' Alliance. ' (Applause.) He did not wish to bind himself or any person in the room to all the details of that Bill.. There were ' points upon which he felt that that bill was defective, and , must remain so until certain legislation had taken place, ' and other points, such as the division of rates, in which the I landlord was asked to pay too large tnd the tenant too small a share. He would not argue upon these details, hut I would content himself with replying to some of the most prominent objections which he had heard during the last few weeks while talking to landlords. The first thing that landlords always told you was, "You are going to reduce our rents to an excessive degree; it is thoroughly unfair to us that such a bill should pass." Why, it seemed to him that by such a bill as this rents would be made fair and just, and must be increased if they were below their pre- sent value. Let him give them a simple, if rather a commonplace, illustration of the position. Suppose that there was some man in Chester who had the monopoly of sailing toast, and who sold this toast to people who bought their own butter, but the law established that when lie had • sold this toast, and after his customers had buttered it, he should have the right to take it back from them and eat it. (Laughter and applause.) If that was so did they think the price of toast would rise? (Renewed laughter.) Put the landlord in the place of the man who sold the toast and the tenant farmer in the place of the man who bought the toast and buttered it, in the shape of , the farm which he improved, and he said that if such an injustice was repeated the price of land would rise. (Applause.) The Duke of Argyll, in his letter to the Economist, said, "We are net going to enter into co-partnership in the land with our tenants; the landlord brings so much into the stock and the tenant brings so much less, and he is not to be admitted on equal terms with us." Why, as far as be could see the Alliance only wanted to remedy the evils of the present co- partnership which existed between landlord and tenant—a co-partnership in which the big partner could swallow up the little partner's share. (Applause.) What they wanted to do by this bill was to keep the landlord's capital and the tenant's capital distinct, to say to the landlord "This is yours," and to the tenant "This is yours," and to give to the tenant, if he wished to separate from his partner, the right of going into the open market and selling his share to some one else. (Cheers.) It was perfectly true that it was impossible to . separate physically from the soil what belonged to the landlord and what belonged to the tenant, but it was possible, as Mr. Barclay had pointed out, for an arbitrator, merely by putting figures together, to show what advantages or disadvantages had accrued to the landlord's farm during the interval since the farm was taken, and that being done, it only remained to do a simple sum in addition to ascertain what belonged to the tenant. The 011,13 mistake in law which had worked all this hardship had been that old Latin legal phrase which, translated, was—that what- ever was put into the freehold belonged to the freehold. Landlords and agents had too frequently borne that phrase in mind, while they' had forgotten that other one of hic, hcec, hoc, which they had learnt at school. (Laughter.) They now wanted them to learn that that old legal maxim was no longer of any effect, and to show that the capital of the tenant farmer when placed in the soil was as secure as when placed in the Bank of England. Mr. Latham then proposed the following resolution ;—That this meeting approves of the principle contained in the Land Bill promoted by the Farmers' Alliauce and explained by Mr. Barclay, inasmuch as by clauses of the hill, firstly, the tenant would possess a marketable security for his unexhatuded improvements, and consequently capital would be safely invested in a holding; secondly, the law of distiess would be abolished and the preferential security given at present to the landlord would no longer either *unduly increase rents or work to the preju- dice of other creditors; thirdly, the payment of tithes by the landlord would make the annual sum payable as rent definite and invariable; fourthly, the rates being 'divided between the landlord und tenant the owner would be more fully acquainted with and in consequence more interested in preventing additional burdens being thrown on the oecu- pier during the term of the tenancy." (Cheers.)—Mr. Dar- byshire, of Little Legh, Seconded the resolution, which was carried unanimously.—Mr. Baxter proposed a vote of thanks to Mr. Barclay for his'address—Mr. J. Tomkinson, in seconding the resolution, said that he could endoree every clause in the Alliance bill with the exception of that giving the farmer free sale of his tenant right, which he thought would operate to the detriment, not to say injustice, of the landlord.—The resolution was passed.

THE ALLEGED BOYCOTTING OF A CHESHIRE

FARMER. Sir,--Referring to your paragraph entitled "A Cheshire farmer's sad history,' the amount owing by him to me was £153 Bs. 6d., and the sale realized £l2B 195. Id. gross, so that lam a considerable loser. The farmer has held the farm, which consists not only of land but of a good house and buildings, and which could have been let at the same rent, many times over, for 19 years, and I have returned in manure dm., daring the term,' £llO, which I can reckon up, and have reduced his rent, during the last two years, by £2 pr Cheshire acre, and alsoreturned him £4O besides. It must not be forgotten that the acre spoken of in your paper is a Cheshire acre, which contains more than double the area of a statute acre, so that the farm is really upwards of 22 statute acres in extent. Having to pay my way in the world, and having a family of seven of my own to provide for, I have to be paid, for I am only a retired farmer, and I can produce, if necessary, papers that will throw a new light upon the subject, and will fully justify me in the action I was compelled to take.—Yours obediently, THE BOYCOTTED CHESHIRE LANDLORD.

IN RE BOSON STREET. Sir,—l recollect hearing tell of a certain Irish M.P. who rose in the " House " to explain that "Ireland was an island entirely surrounded by the say." Now, although Robson- street is not quite in that predicament, still it almost sur- rounded by water left by recent rains. Although tenanted by respectable ratepayers living in decent cottage houses, it seems to be a place entirely forgotten, either by the property owners or the body corporate. It is quite destitute of drains for carrying off the water, also it is a very difficult matter to liteer your way up the street on a dark night for want of a gas lamp. In fact, I should judge there is not a street in Warrington in as bad a condition. When we go to bed at night, we, as Christians, certainly pray for mercy, but we do not expect our prayers to be answered so literally, by having a miniature Mersey rolling before our doors in the morning. The street for some time has been almost full of water the humidity arising from which has a tendency to give coughs, colds, asthmas, and all the other "ills that flesh is heir to every one who lives there, when we step out of our doors we have to explore the shores to find some narrow isthmus, by which we can get into Manchester-road. If, as a private road, the Corporation have nothing to do with its repair, I should think they have something to do with requesting the property owners to do it. It may be that we have done some- thing wrong that we are saddled with the nuisance; but, my dear sir, if you could see the condition we are in some morn- ing when the" tide" is up, you would pity us, and at least saylf the thing cannot be altered a boat ought to be pro- vided, whereby we may be wafted to the other shore.— Your, dm -A SUFFERER. --

THE BURIALS ACT. Sir,—Will you kindly allow space for the following facts? —which are not as widely known among the poor of War- rington as they ought to be, viz., that Dissenters under the " Barials Laws Amendment Act, 1881," have the right- to bury on church ground, without the rites of the Church of England, but to secure this right n9tice of 48 hours must be given to the clergyman in charge of the parish. Last Sun- day afternoon I was asked to bury a child (one of my own Sunday scholars) on church ground, the parents having a very strong desire that I should do so. I went to the ceme- tery, but feund out after being there some time that the con- ditions of the Act had not been complied with. These facts were communicated to the parents and the officiating clergy- man, with the result that, after being there for over an hour, I came home without being able to bury the child, which was done by the church clergyman. I think it is time the Burial Board took steps to let it be known what the law is on this point, as it is not to be expected that poor people are acquainted with Acts of Parliament. In the above instance, if anyone is to blame it i the parents of the child for not giving.the required notice, but it seems hard when one el your scholars die, whose mother is a mein- of your own congregation, that the person chosen by the parents to bury their dead cannot do so, because, through igno- rance, the letter of law is not complied with. It ought also to be made known that Dissenters do not claim this right for the sake of the fee, as this, by law, goes to the Church clergymen—even when the Dissenter has buried the dead— which to my mind is not very satisfactory. • A. SMITH, Cockhedge.

WARRINGTON COUNTY PETTY SESSIONS.. WEDNESDAY.—Before Messrs. John Rylands and Robert Houghton. YOUTHFUL OnsTntorrosors.—Three youths, named Elijah Poole, John Thomas Poole, and Frederick Molyneux, were summoned for obstructing the free passage of a public footpath near Penketh, on the 20th November last, by stand- ing thereon.—P. C. Rogers proved the case, and said he had had endless complaints about these lads, whom he bad cautioned scores of times, but it had been of no use:—The Bench said this was a great nuisance, and the defendants were fined 3s. each, including costs. BREACHES OF THE LICENSING ACT.—MiChael Scully Was charged with having, on Sunday, the 27th November, at Orford, unlawfully sold a quart of beer during prohibited hours, and Owen Davies was charged with aiding and abetting. Scully was further charged with refusing to admit the police.—P. S. Pattinson said he was in Orford at five minutes past 11 on tho night of the day in question, when he saw the front door of the defendant Scully's shop open a litte, and immediately they had passed Owen came out with a can of beer. They got the can from him and took him back to the shop door, which had been closed. They knocked several times and, called out, but Scully did not open the door.—ln reply to the clerk, the sergeant said they did not say who they were. This the clerk said they ought to have done.—Scully, who pleaded guilty to the first charge, was fined 40s. and costs, and Davies was fined ss. and costs. SUNDAY SportTneo.—Joseph Jones, who said he was a labourer, was summoned for having, on the 13th November, conamitteed a trespass in the day time on land in the posses- sion of George Seger, at Penketh, in search of game.—P.C. Rogers said on Sunday, the 13th ultimo, he heard shots, and on proceeding to ascertain whence they arose, he saw the defendant standing behind a hedge in Mr. Segar's field with a gun under his arm.—Mr. Seger said this sort of thing had become a nuisancs.—The clerk: These pecple think the holding of a gun license entitles them to go about shooting 'anything anywhere.—Defendant was fined 50 and costs, and the Bench hoped it would be a warning to him. "Too READY To BELIEVE EVIL."---Tobn Smith was summoned for having, on the Ist inst., at Newton, assaulted and beaten his wife Margaret. The defendant pleaded "guilty to saucing her but not to beating her."—Com- plainant said her husband got up on the morning of the Ist inst. and called her" everything his tongue could that was had," then gave her a "stroke," and said he would strangle her. Her life was in danger, as defendant had threatened her both night and day. Defendant was sober at the time. Jealousy, for which there was no ground, was the cause of his ill-treatment. —A neighbour stated she saw complainant on the let Met, and her neck bore marks as though defen- dant had bad his fingers about her throat.—Complainant asked for a separation order, but this the Bench could not grant. This was the defendant's second offence, and he was committed for one month. KNOCKED Dows BY HIS WlFE—James Bond, a young man, was charged with having, on the 19th and 20th ult., at Sankey, assaulted his wife.—Defendant pleaded " inn o- cent.”—Complainant said her husband would not give her any money and when she spoke to him he hit her about .the face with his fists.—Defendant stated on the other hand, that his wife (who seemed the stronger of the two) put him on the floor, kneeled upon him, an¢ commenced fighting.—The Bench paid it appeared curious defendant should charge complainant with knocking .khim down and keeping him down; but it was a case in which both parties were to blame, and the Bench dismissed it. ALLEGED CRIMINAL ASSAULT AT EARLESTOWN.—James Singleton, a married man, residing at Grolbarne, was charged with having criminally assaulted a girl named Emma Broom on Saturday ni4ht last, at Earlestown.—On Saturday the prosecutrix left her father's house at Newton to go to Earlestown, sad was proceeding along the footpath by the side of the railway when she met prisoner, who got hold of her, but she screamed and got away. She ran in the direction of Earles- town, and he followed her, and caught her in the wicket gate at Park-road, where he 'committed the offence with which he was charged. Proseeutrix afterwards ran back towards Newton and met a man, to whom she com- plained, and he took her home. Informttion was after- wards given to the police, and the prisoner was apprehended. —The prisoner, who was defended by lily. G. T. Moore, was committed to the Assizes for trial.
PRESENTATION TO A VOLUNTEER
OFFICER AT PRESCOT.

On Tuesday evening, a very interesting gathering of volunteers and others took place at the Assembly Rooms, Derby-street, Present, the occasion being the presentation of a solid silver sugar basin with tongs and cream jug, of unique and elegant design and workmanship, in handsome morocco leather, to Captain Cross, who has for a large number of years devoted much time and labour to the in- terest and well-being of the volunteer movement in the town. The present, which was supplied by Mr. Thos. Prescott, of Stanley Crescent, Prescot, was Subscribed for by non-com- missioned officers and men of the late 48th (Present) L.R.V., now forming EC company of the 21st (St. Helens) L.R.V., as a token of the respect and esteem in which he is held by them. The inscription was as follows: "Presented to Captain Henry Cross, by the non-com- missioned officers and men of the late 48th L.R.V., as a taken of their high esteem and respect, 3rd December, 1881."—Co1our-Sergeant Scotson presided, and delivered an appropriate speech. Other speeches followed.

div.head: IRON AND COAL TRADES.
div.p: IRON AND COAL TRADES.

LANCASHIRE, M'ednesday.—Although the coal trade of r this district is probably in as fairly good a position as might reasonably be expected under the exceptional circumstances , resulting from the large stocks token in by consumers a month or so back, and the unusual mildness of the weather which has since prevailed, the present depressed state of the market is making itself seriously felt. For all descriptions of fuel for house fire purposes the demand is extremely dull, and the bulk of the collieries have had to go on short time, whilst there has been a large accumulation of stocks. The leading colliery proprietors are mostly still holding for late rates; but there has been a giving way on the part of more needy coalowners, and the market is unquestionably easier, buyers for prompt delivery being in many cases able to place out orders at Gd. per ton under the prices which were ruling last month. Common classes of round coal, although more plentiful in the market owing to the lessened requirements for house fire consumption, are, however, still in tolerably good demand :or iron making and steam purposes; and engine classes of fuel also meet with a fairly good enquiry, with prices if anything rather firmer, owing to the present limited production of slack. The average prices at which coal can be bought at the pit mouth may be given as under: Best coal, Ps 6d. to 10s., with second qualities ranging from To. 6d. to Bs. 6d., and common round coal from Gs. to 7s. per ton; good burgy averages about 55., good slack 45. to 4s. 3d. per ton; and common qualities about 3s. to 3s. 6d. per ton. In the shipping trade there has been very little doing, not so much, perhaps, from the actual absence of orders as from the scarcity of vessels owing to the recent stormy weather, and there has been a good deal of pressure to sell at low figures, steam coal being offered for delivery at the high level, Liver- pool or at Garston, at prices ranging from 7s. 61 to Bs. per ton. For coke there is a continued fair demand, at late rates. In the iron trade there has been a considerable amount of activity during the past week. The large reduction of stocks in the north of England and the upward movement in out- side markets have, no doubt tendei towards an increased anxiety on the part of consumers to cover forward require- ments, and during the last fow days there as been a consider- able business doing in pig inn. As the result of the toler- ably large sales which have been made and the increased demand on the part of buve s, the market has grown decidedly firmer, and makers are very indifferent about book- ing further orders for extended delivery. For Lancashire pig iron a considerably increased demand is repotted, and local makers who have plenty of orders in band for the present could sell largely into next year. In face, however, of the upward tendency of the market they are not inclined to book orders for forward delivery to the extent which buyers are offering, and although local brands of pig iron are without change in price from last week, sellers are very stiff at the full rates of 495., less 2, for both forge and foundry qualities, delivered equal to Manchester, with a decided tendency to advance upon these figures should the market maintain its presen,t position. In outside brands of pig iron, such as Lincolnshire and Derbyshire, considerable sales have taken place, and prices generally have gone up during the last few days, most of the makers now asking advances of Is. to 2s. per ton upon last week's rates, the average quotation for delivery into the Manchester district being now about 495. to 50s. per ton, less 2L Finished iron makers continue very busy, with a good deal of inquiry coming in for next year, which, however, is only being entertained to a very limited extent. Prices for manufac- tured iron aro a'so firmer all round, and £6 12s. ed. to £6 15s. per ton are now the average quotations for bars delivered into the manchester district.

div.head: FRODSITAAL
div.p: FRODSITAAL

CONCERT AT FnonstrAor.—An amateur concert was given in the Town Hall, Frodsham, on Monday evening, by a party of ladies and gentlemen from Bowdon and Manchester, in aid of the Frodsham Parish Church Organ Fund. There was a good audience, which included the elite of the neigh- bourhood. The following programme was rendered :—Part song, "My true love bath my heart" (Smart) ; song, "The wandering minstrel" (Mazzoni), Dr. Simpson ; duet, "The sailor sighs" (Balfe), Miss Winward and Mr. Mayson; song, "My love has gene " (Molloy), Mrs. Mayson; part • song, "Since first I saw your face" (Ford); pianoforte solo, "Prelude, sarabande, and gigue " (Corelli), Mr. J. W. Side- bothain ; song, "The yeoman's wedding song " (Prince Poniatowski), Mr. Gilliat ; duet, "O'er the hills, o'er the vale" (S. Glover), Miss Winward au' Mrs. Mayson; madri- gal,"Now, 0 now, I needs mnst pert" (Dowland); part song, "Come live with me " (Sir W. G. Bennett) ; song, "Killarney " (Balfe). Miss Winward ; trio, " Up, quit thy bower" (B. Richards), Miss A. M. Simpson, Rev. E. F. Leach, and Mr. Gilliat ; song, "Tom Bowling" (C. Diblin), Dr. Simpson ;* pianoforte solo, Mr. J. W. Sidenotham ; song, "In a distant land" (Tauber°, Miss A. M. Simpson; song, "The message " (Blumenthal), Rev. E. F. Leach ; quartette, " The rose of the valley" (Knyrett), Miss Winward, Mrs. Mayson, Rev. E. F. Leach, Dr. Simpson; glee, "The fisher- man's goodnight" (Bishop) ; National Anthem. The pro- gramme contained many pleasing features, and tve various pieces were given with finish and precision, the encores being numerous and gracefully responded to. The part songs were very well balanced throughout. It would difficult to -single out any particulae of the programme for special commenda- tion where such uniform excellence was attrined, in fact we should be inclined to reserve our praise for the selection of the songs, ctc., the theme and spirit of the words being most beautiful, and many of them being given for the first time in Frodsham.

- --- -- PRESIDENT. The following letter was read by the SEertrrany (Mr. Thomas Rigby) : " Whimaleigh. Garstang, November 12, 1881.—Dear Sir,— I have to acknowledge the recei,,t of your letter of the 11th. In which you inform me that the Royal 111anche.ster, Liverpool, and North Lancashire Agricultural Society have elected me as thelr chairman for the ensuing year. The state of my health has prevented me from fulfilling my duty as one of the Council during the past year, which I very much regret. for I have always felt the deepest interest in the society, of one branch of I which I have been a member for more than half a century. I will do my best, if the future state of my health should enable me to fulfil the duty of the offix to which lain now elected., and it `will be an especial pleasure to me to preside over the dinner at the time of the Preston Guild, which will be the fourth guild which I shall have atter,ded, if I live so long. Yotus faithfully, Wes MAItLEIGII, Thomas Itigby:'

THE REDUCTION OF R&IINFLYTiE. Mr. limy reported that a letter had been recelsed from Mr. Jenkins (Secretary to the Royal Agricultural Society), in regard to the redaction of railway rates for cattle and horses. The members would recollect that at a previous meeting it was decided that the society should take action on the matter. He'had considered that the best step would be to get the Royal Agricultural Society and other arricutr tural associations to combine with them; and the COM* niunication from Mr. Jenkins showed that the Royal was willing to do so. As the members knew, the greatest out- cry in regard to this matter was from the exhibitors of horses. Perhaps it would be as well that a deputation from the society should be appointed to wait upon the railway companies. It was decided that the Chairman, the Hon. Wilbraham Egerton M.P., Messrs. T. Rigby, R. Whalley, and J. Halsall should be appointed the deputation, with power to add to their number.

PAPERS BY MEMBERS. • The SECRETARY said he had prepared a scheme of prizes for the considefation of the members. Amongst the papers which had been written for circulation amongst the mem- bers was a report as to the state of agricul&ip in the north east of the society's district, by Mr. R. ls7lloward. He might also remind them that it had been decided by the council that a report of the state of agriculture should be written annually in the particulardistrict where the society's show was held. It was desirable that members should in the mean time, think of some one who was fit to write such a toped. There was also a paper by Mr. Smetham, on the economic use of agricultural manure; and a report of the dairy trials at Blackburn. ALTERATION OF TIME OF CLOSING THE SHOW. After a brief conversation, it was resolved that the show should be closed each day at four o'clock, instead of at six.

PRESTON AND THE SHOW. The SECRETARY stated that he had a letter from the Town Clerk of Preston, stating that, if possible, a deputation from that town would attend the meeting that day for the pur- pose of discussing the allotment of the special prizes; or if they could not attend, they would write. As to the public luncheon, he considered that it might harmonize better with the action of the Guild Committee to have it oil the Wed. nesday instead of on the Tuesday. . It was resolved that it should be left to the Guild Como rnittee to decide which was the more suitable day. STEWARDS AND THE JErDGEs. • Mr. RODGERS considered that there was ground for cont. plaint in the fact that the stewards frequently went up to the judges whilst they were going on with their work. Thin ought not to be permitted; and he might say he had heard of cases where stewards had pointed out many defects with regard to animals. Many shows had a rule that stewards should not speak to the judges unless they were spoken to, and only then in cases where their remarks were not likely to effect the impartiality of the judges. The CHAIRMAN: Does not that rather effect the judge himself? Mr. RODGERS : The judge cannot very well get out of the way of the steward. It is a very difficult thing for him to say to a steward" You should not talk to me." A MEMBER: I hope you will not say that has occurred in connection with this society. Mr. RODGERS. I know that it has occurredin connection with this society. I like to be plain when lam speaking. The SECRETARY: We might put down that it should be one of the instructions to the stewards to avoid speaking to the judges except where it is absolutely necessary. This suggestion was agreed ELECTION OF TEI COUNCIL. After some discussion as the desirability of sending out voting papers to members in the election of the Council, it was resolved, on the motion of Mr. RALSALL, seconded by Mr. PETER BLUNDELL, that the voting should be carried out at the general meeting.

div.head: JUDGING OF FARMS.
div.p: JUDGING OF FARMS.
- DISCUSSION AS TO JUDGES FOR SIIEEP, DOGS, ETC. Mr. BLUNDELL remarked that he was inclined to think that one judge in _respect to farms would be better than several.

—.,.-.. The Sacrum:my wee of opinion that one judge was quite as capable of doing the work as two or more. He con- sidered the Royal Society erred by appointing teo many judges. Eight members voted :for the amendment, and six for the original motion, which was, therefore, declared lost. Mr. CerrEmr. moved that one judge only be appointed for farms.

FATAL ACCIDENT AT ST. HELENS RAILWAY STATION.. On Tuesday night, a fatal accident occurred at the St. Helens Station of the London and North-Western Railway, whereby a middle-aged, respectably-attired woman was killed. Deceased, who was the wife of a tradesman named Holcroft, residing in Wal!gate, Wigan, arrived in St. Helens by the 5-44 p.m. train from Wigan. She proceeded to the level crossing at the back of the train, put up her umbrella, and was seen to stand at the edge of the crossing. Just at tbis moment the slow train from Southport to Ditton was drawing to the platform, and deceased, without noticing it apparently made a start to cross. The driver felt an ob- struction, and got off his engine to ascertain the cause. The unfortunate woman was then found in the four-foot, bleed. lug badly from wound in the head. On being raised, she breathed for a few seconds and then expired. Her body was carried into the porters' room, and the police authorities having arrived, she was taken to the public mortuary in Foundry-street. Deceased's umbrella, broken and doubled up, was found on the line near the place, BA was also a small basket containing provisions. In her dress pocket WU third-class ticket from Wigan to St. Helens, a handkerchief bearing the name of "E. Litherland," and on her person WU a gold watch bearing the maker's, name, "John Thwaites, Penrith," with an imitation gold chain. On further examla. tog the garments, :bunch of small keys, a retch key, and a purse containing about £lO 15s. in gold and silver were found in the skirt pocket.—An inquest was held on Thurs- day, on the body of Jane Floicroft, 52 years of age.—Thos. Ifolcroft, tailor and clogger, 144, Wallgate, Wigan, said deceased was his wife. She left horns on Tuesday afternoon to go to St. Helens to nurse her sick sister. Witness went with her a portion of the way to the station, shook hands with her, and said good bye. She was in good-bye. She was in good health and spirits. Oa the following day P.C. Peebles showed him several articles which he knew his wife had taken with her, and on going to St.. Helens identified the body of his wife. She knew about the steps over the line, but being stoutly built, and at 'times asthmatical, she avoided them whenever she ' could. Witness appeared to be in great distress and hurt that the body of his wife should have been taken to the .üblic mortuary; it was the worst place they could have aken her to.—Mr. Lees, solicitor, Wigan appeared on be. half of the relatives of the deceased, and sad that though the building bore the words "public mortuary," it would be better styled a public disgrace, as the windows were t broken in, and he believed it was frequented by rats.—Mr. Moss, the station master, said that the accident took place at the crossing neatest leainford. He believed she stepped I on the line, and was waiting for a goods train to move off , the other line, when the train from Rainford knocked her down.—A verdict of "Accidental death" was returned.

div.head: PRESCOT MAN CHARGED WITH EMBEZZLEMENT. •
div.p: A PRESCOT MAN CHARGED WITH EMBEZZLEMENT. •

At the Preecot Police Court, on Thursday forenoon, be. ore Mr. W. L. Evans, a young man named George Brown. bill, a native of Prescot, was charged under warrant with having embezzled three sums of money amounting alta gether to £2 12s. 9d., the property of Mr. Thomas Prescott, watch material manufacturer, Stanley Crescent, Prescof, in whose employ the prisoner had been as traveller. The prisoner, who was apprehended at Accrington on Wednes- day, was remanded for a week.

div.head: EXAMINER.
div.p: THE EXAMINER.
SATURDAY, DECEMBER 10, 1881.

IBETAND continues in a state of unsettlement incal- culably predjudicial to the material interests of its own people, and not a little disturbing to the whole nation. By every means which are at its command, the Queen's Government is doing its very utmost to prevent crime, to enforce the laws, to stem the torrent of revolution- ary agitation, and to convince as many Irishmen as have not entirely lost their heads that the Government is not an enemy but a friend, determined to give to the tillers of the soil of Ireland, and to other industrial interests, all necessary protection against oppression and injustice. The position of the Executive in Ire- land may be likened to that of the driver of a vehicle whose horse, usually restive and given to shying, has taken fright, and has set off at a headlong gallop. The animal is madly rushing towards destruction, and nothing can prevent a smash but the nerve and firm- ness of the driver. If he can keep his seat, and a light rein, with sufficient control over the horse to keep his head straight and tho vehicle in the width of the roadway, the brute will before long become ex- hausted by his great pace, and will be stopped without serious mishap. But should the driver be thrown, or lose all control, the destruction of horse and vehicle, by violent collision with some rigid obstacle, is all but certain. Ireland is the runaway horse, which, if left to its own frantic course, would. hurl itself to perdition. And if the driver, which is the responsible Govern- ment, should lose firm grasp of the reins, its frustra- tion would be the signal for a calamitous overture of the entire social structure. It is the duty of the authorities to hold on with plucky tenacity until the taming effect of exhaustion has begun to operate upon the subversive organisations in Ireland typified by the horse whiCh, in vernacular phrase, has "taken bog- gart." These troubles which are convulsing Ireland are no new experience for that unhappy people. History never repeated itself so often, or so closely, as in the periodical occurrence. of agrarian outrages and seditious movements in Ireland. The events which lead up to them have generally been natural more than the results of human action. Bad seasons, ruined crops, potatoe blights, break-down of tenant farming under the crushing incubus of rack-rents, and gaunt famine as the sequel of all lesser distresses and mis- fortunes—these have been the originating causes of those Irish curses which have been most acute and longest in their duration. There is not a country in the world in which the same grievous sufferings and privations would not have led to popular discontent, agitation against unjust laws and systems of labour. The English Tory, who has the shortest memory of any man on earth, for historical occurrences which do not fit in with his party cry of the moment, may please to forget that there were disturbances in Ireland more severe than the present all through those years of unchallenged Tory rule from 1777 to 1880 ; again in 1803, again in 1833, again in 1848, again in 1866-7. when the Fenian conspiracy ripened into rebellion (a Conservative Government being in power), and besides the bloodshed in Ireland, those terrible outrages in the streets of Manchester, and in Clerkenwell, London, were perpetrated. There may be fresh phases de- veloped by each succeeding upheaval of Irish dis- affection, but the same conditions of precariousness of tenure of Irish farmers and grinding poverty of Irish labourers provoked them all. Those conditions are not of the Liberal party's making. We will not say they are either of the Conservative party's making. They have grown out of a past history made up of constant rebellions, worked by blood-thirsty atrocities, and as constant reconquests, not less ruthless in their attendant incidents. Henry the Second, Henry the Seventh, Elizabeth, Cromwell, William the Third, George the Third., each in turn undertook and carried out with many bloody episodes the pacification of Ireland, each after the peculiar fashion of the ruler and of the age. And the Irish situation as we see it now, is the result of the combined measures in dealing with the insurgent Irish race of English monarchs and their ministers for seven or eight centuries. Nobody living now is accountable for it. But we have all got to face its dangers and its eventualitiet And where we think the Liberal party has a clever conscience in reference to the conflict of races still going on in Ireland than the Conservative party, is that whilst the latter has attempted nothing worth naming to redress Irish wrongs, the Liberal party has made the most persistent and untiring endeavours to atone for past misgovernment, so far as it can be atoned for, and to reconcile Irishmen to the British Union by abolishing the badges of ascendancy,—the State Church of a small and largely alien minority, and the unchecked despotic sway of a small, absentee class of landlords. Every man in this world encounters instances of wrong and iniquitous abuse; but it is the earnest Reformer above who does his best to right the wrong, to requite the wronged, to root out the scandalous abuse. We Liberals claim to have effected this, to the utmost of our strength, in the remedial legislation we have passed for Ireland, thanks to the genius and energy of our noble statesmen, Mr. Glad- stone conspicuous amongst them. The Tories seem to hate us for having accomplished these great acts of justice, much, we fear, from the same evil motives that compelled Cain to hate and to slay his brother, I "because his own works were evil, ani his brother's righteous." But Tory enmity will never make Liberals regret having given to Ireland religious equality and security of holding to the honest tenant farmer. No, nor will the apparent failure of many Irishmen to appreciate as it deserves all that Liberal statesmen have wrought in their behalf ever make us repeat the policy of redress, or grudge the enormous toil our illustrious leaders and our representatives in Parliament have bestowed upon the Irish Church Act of 1869, and the Land Acts of 1870 and 1881. Time will indicate that the Liberal party's maxims of Irish administration. If" a corrupt tree cannot bring forth good fruit; neither can a .good tree bring forth evil fruit." The tree of equitable legislation for Ireland has only been planted yesterday; it is but a sapling as yet, but it will grow, and nurtured by all natural influences it will at last become a great and fruitful tree, like unto that seen in the apostolic vision ''whose leaves were for the healing of the nations."

TILE enthusiastic demonstration of Liberals which took place at the Public Hall, on Wednesday, must have convinced the most sceptical that the thee when Warrington will be content to be misrepresented by a Tory has entirely passed away, and that the popu- larity of our worthy borough member, Mr. J. G. McMinnies, is as great, if not greater, than ever it was. That the vast audience which crowded every available spot in that large hall were entirely in accord with the Liberal principles enunciated that night was patent from the hearty applause which greeted the utterances of the three Liberal M.P.'s, who spoke on the most important topics of the day. Tho unanimity and enthusiasm with which the vote of confidence in Mr. McMinnies was carried showed

div.head: EXAMINER, SATURDAY DECEMBER 10, 1881.
div.p: THE EXAMINER, SATURDAY DECEMBER 10, 1881.

that the Liberal party are thoroughly satisfied with the way in which our representative has discharged the duties devolving upon him, and the only fault—if it be a fault—that was found in him was that he has devoted himself to such a close attendance in the House as to endanger his own health. As a matter of course, since Irish affairs occupied such a large proportion of the time of Parliament during the last

session, and the passing of the Irish Land Bill was the principal item of legislation, these were prominent topics in Mr. McMinnies's annual address. It has been universally admitted that the Irish Land Act was a piece of very important legislation, inasmuch as it has given to the down-trodden people of the sister isle fixity of tenure at a fair rent, and secured to the tenant farmer "the reward that his own industry deserves in the value of the land which his own labour and capital have made valuable." An Act that has been passed with this object in view certainly deserves a fair trial, and we believe that Mr. McMinnies spoke the sentiments of every true hearted Liberal when he said "that the Land Act with the influence of time,

and with the redress of other grievances that exist in Ireland, will bring about the day when Irishmen will be glad to stand side by side with Englishmen or Scotchmen, proud te possess equal powers or equal privileges in the government of this great and united nation." Passing on to the question of Fair Trade, Mr. McHinnies veryclearly showed the fallacy of the idea that it was possible for us to improve our com- mercial prospects by returning to the old system of Protection, and pointed out how the country had greatly increased in prosperity since Free Trade had been established. Referring to the state of trade under the Tory Government, and comparing it with the present, he said that two or three years ago half the looms and spindles in Lancashire employed in the production of cotton goods were idle, and half the rest only working three or four days a week, whereas now there is not a tangle loom or spindle idle, employment is plentiful, wages have risen, and will rise, and this is true of other trades. There cannot be a doubt-that since the present Go- vernment came into power confidence has been re- stored amongst capitalists and commercial men generally, and with a policy of peace instead of war and bluster trade has improved, and will continue to improve notwithstanding a few bad seasons. A Goverftment that has therefore by a peaceful policy contributed to the improvement that has taken place in commerce is well worthy of the support of all those who are interested in the prosperity of the country— and whole not?—and by upholding that Government Mr. McMinnies has merited a continuance of the con- fidence that was reposed in him by the ratepayers of Warrington at the last election, and we hope the day is far distant when he will cease to be the representa-

tive of Warrington in the British House of Commons. Mr. Jesse Collings, M.P., for Ipswich, who is a well- known Radical of the Birmingham school, followed with an able and elequent address on the necessity of Land Law Reform, and the need which exists for giving to the agricultural labourers of this country an interest in the soil. In glowing and heart-stirring language he depicted the evil results of the present system of land monopoly which obtains in England, showing how it has the effect not only of grinding down the earnings of the farm labourers, and driving them into the towns to compete with their fellow- workmen, and thus reduce the wages of the artizans, biet also that it was the means of increasing the pauperism which exists amongst us to a very large extent. Mr. Collings has evidently given the subject careful attention, and as this question is rapidly coming to the front, we shall expect to see him taking no unimportant part in the agitation which must pre- cede legislation thereon. That our old townsman, Mr. Peter Rylands, agreed with the sentiments of Mr. Collings was evident from the sarcastic manner in which he referred to the actions of the landowners in the House of Lords, and it was with feelings of pleasure that we noticed that he, as the former Liberal member for the borough, and an old Warringtonian, had been selected to move the vote of confidence in Mr. McMinnies. In the struggle which will eventu- ally take place with the great landowning class on the alteration of the land laws, we may be sure to find Messrs McMinnies, Collings, and Rylands standing shoulder to shoulder in endeavouring to secure such legisla- tion on this subject as will tend to promote the greatest happiness to the greatest number of the people of this country. The struggle with the great landowners to secure the passing of the Irish Land Act was a long one, but is nothing compared to the struggle which is before us in the attempt to obtain such an alteration of the English Land Law as will enable the agricultural labourer to have an interest in the soil. The landowning classes will fight very bard before they will give up any of the great privileges which they have enjoyed for so many years, and it will therefore be necessary to educate the people thoroughly on the subject, and to give to our es- teemed member, Mr. MeMinnies, and his Liberal col - leagues, all the support in our power.

of England during the last 50 years; and there is not a doubt that if the Education Act of 1874 had not been passed, notwithstanding the fiercest opposition on the part of the Tories and the other lovers of denominational educa- tion, our supremacy in nianufacture would gradually have died out. Ignorance is the mother of crime, and the more children of the boat people class are neglected, and left to themselves like veritable Ishmaelites, the more rope stealing and other cases there will be in years to come. The Frodsham Parish Church Organ Fund will benefit by the concert which was given in the Town Hall, Frodsham, on Monday, and the Restoration Committee are much in- debted to Miss Simpson, of Dunsdale, for commencing, what I hope is to be a series of musical entertainments, in aid of the funds for the completion of the restoration of the Parish Church. It may be explained that the funds for the restora- tion of the fabric of the church, and for providing an organ for the efficient rendering of the musical portion of the ser- vice are entirely distinct, as there is an endowment which exists for defraying the salary of the organist, &c. ; and ttie surplus funds now amount to about £l6O, which amount has been offered by the trustees of the organ lot as a nucleus for a fund to purchase a new organ. The fund now stands as follows :—Surplus fund as above, £160; sale of old organ, £45; the Misses Fawcett, £25; Seaton Taylor Esq , £1; John Ti. Hayes Esq £5O; a late parishioner, £5O; interest, £1 2s. 7d.; total, £332 2s. 7d. The friends of the game of Polo will be glad to hear that a club has Seen formed in Widnes, and the first game will be played on the 26th instant, on the field belonging to the Football Club.
FLACCUS.
ILUNCORN MADRIGAL CLUB.—The members of this club will give their next concert on the 23rd instant, and the subject will be "The Messiah."

HALTON PARISH CHURCH MuruaT IMPROVEMENT SOCIETY.—A meeting was held in connection with this society on Tuesday evening. Mr. Wright occupied the chair. Mr. Tandy read a paper, entitled "The duty of lay- men," at the conclusion of which the following members gave their views on the subject :—Mr. J. Brown, T. Wright, J. Hancock and, H. Thompson. A vote of thanks to the essayist was proposed by Mr. Hancock, and seconded by Mr. Potter, and one to the chairman was proposed by Mr. Brown and seconded by Mr. Thomason. Lady Brooke and Miss Brooke were present during the prcceedings. SERVICE OF SONG AT WIDNES.—A service of song, en- titled the "Babes in the Basket," was given at the Primitive Methodist Chapel, Widnes, on Monday evening. Mr, S. Owens occupied the chair, and the Rev. T. Peters was the reader. Mr. Seddon conducted the musical portion of the service. There was a good attendance. The service was repeated on Wednesday evening at the Simm's Cross chapel, when the proceeds were devoted to the chapel funds. The Rev. J. Morton, of War- rington, superintendept of the circuit, occupied the chair on the second occasion, and Mr. Drought, of Widnes, was the reader.

GOOD TEMPLARY AT WinxEs.—On Wednesday evening, a meeting of the members of the Star Lodge, 1.0.G.T., was held in the lodge room, Mersey-road, to consider the desire- bill' of holding at an early da'e a week's temperance mis- sion, to consist of a series of entertainments, &c., in different parts of the town ; an entertainment to take place each night, and the series to be continued for a week. Mr. Res- call occupied the chair, and there were about 30 persons present, including the members of the Star Lodge, and depu- tations from the Hope of Appleton Lodge, the Good Samari- tan Lodge, and the Haste to the Rescue Lodge. It was suggested that the proposed week's mission should be held about Christmas, as the efforts of temperance workers were then specially needed, but no final decision was come to on the point.

A CARELESS MOTILE R AT RIINCORN.—Mr. Ridgway, coroner, held in inquest at the Anchor Inn, Runcorn, on Thursday, on the body of a child named Alice O'Neil, aged 2,1 years, whose mother lives at 7, Mill-street, Runcorn. It appeared that the child had been suffeling from inflammation for a con- siderable length of time, but no medical assistance had been given or applied for within the past three weeks. On Mon- day the child died. A post-mortem examination was made on Tuesday by Mr. Robinson, who found that the child had died from inflammation of the lungs. It was stated to the coroner that the mother of the child was an intemperate woman. She, however, told the coroner that she had not money to pay for the attendance of a doctor. The Coroner attributed the death of the child in a great measure to the negh ct of the mother, and severely censured her. If she had no money she ought to have applied at once to the relieving officer, who would have been bound to enquire into the case, and, if necessary, give an order for medical attendance.—A verdict of "Natural causes" was returned. BOYCOTTING AT WIENES.—It appears that the other day an Irishman, living in Grentield-street, Widnes, had his goods offered for sale by auction, they having been seized under a distress *warrant. The auctioneer arrived at the spot in due course, and was about to sell the things when the agent of the local Land League interfered and told him that ho must not sell them. At the same time several Irish people in the crowd called out that they would smash every article that he sold, and threatened intended purchasers. The auctioneer remonstrated with the peopte and then sent for the police, but they, however, did not arrive. He then went to see the landlord, who said that the woman owed about £4 for rent. The landlord offered to compromise the matter on payment of 305., but the Irish people in the crowd refused I to hear of this, and said that he might very well let the j woman stay in the house. After several ineff.'.ctual attempts to commence the sale it was abandoned, and the things were subsequently removed and sold in another part of the town

RUNGOBN PABLTA MEN VARY DEBATING SOCIETY.— There was a very scanty attendance at the weekly meeting of this society on Tuesday evening, in conscquence of the inclement weather which prevailed, and also from the fact that there were several other meetings and entertainments in the town at which many of the members were engaged. The speaker therefore suggested that the meeting be adjourned until next Tuesday, which was agreed to.—The member for Warrington gave notice that he would ask the Home Secretary if his attention had been drawn to the published report of a forced sale on a farm in Cheshire, and the circumstances connected with it; also if it be true that the landlord was holding a farm in the neighbourhood at £3 per acre, while the rent charged for the former was £8 per acre; and further, if the government is prepared to in- troduce a Land Bill. for England.—The leader of the Oppo- ..

sition gave notice that he w—ould ask the Solicitor-Gen.e.ral if his attention had been drawn to the recent ruling in respect to the lodger franchise in the law courts, and whether it is the intention of Her Majesty's Government to give effect to the orig.jual intention (in respect of qualifica- tion) of the act relating to lodgers. RITIN.TCORN BURIAL BOARD. —The monthly meeting was held in the Board-room at the Cemetery, on Wednesday afternoon. Mr. Coleburne occupied the chair, and there were also present, Messrs. Rhodes, Moss, Whittaker, Handley Littler, and Salkelcl (secretary.) The report showed that the interments for the month ending November 25th, were 21, corresponding month last year 26, decrease 5; interments for 8 months ending November 25th, were 159; for the cor- responding period last year, 210, showing a decrease in the death-rate of 51. The secretary reported that £240 had been received from the overseers for sinking fund account and current expenses. The receipts from March 25th, to Novem- her2sth, were £l5O Gs. 10d.; for the corresponding period last year £169 sa. 8d , decrease £lB 188.101 The accounts amounting to £2O Ils. sd. were passed, and interest amount- in," to £3B Os, Id., and a cheque ordered to be drawn on sinking fund account for £3O, making with the £l2O re- ceived from the overseers £l5O to pay the balance of mort- gage for £950. The monthly cash account and the inscrip- tions for the head-stones were examined and passed. Six certificates of purchased graves were also signed; Three mortgages for £BOO, latch had been prepared were examined by the Board and found correct. The seal of the Board was attached to them and they were then situed by the chair- man and two members of the Board.—lt was resolved. on Ithe motion of Mr. Rhodes, seconded by Mr. Whittaker, that a Finance and General Purposes Committee be formed, con- sisting of the following members :—Messrs. Coleburn, Moss, ILittler, and Handley. It was also decided that this coin- ' mittee should meet half an hour before the general Board. This concluded the business.

MEnsEY BrissioNs TO SEAmEN, Rtmonx BRANCH.— On Tuesday evening, a miscellaneous entertainment was given in the Regent-street schoolroom, Runcorn, in connec- tion with the above missions. Mr. Thomas Cooke, of the Young Men's Christian Association, presided, and, in his opening remarks, stated the object of the entertainment was to raise funds towards building a missionary house for Mr. Shaw, in connection with the Mersey Mission. He thought Mr. Aaw, in his capacity as seaman's missionary, was as equally entitled to be provided with a free house as the various ministers of the town. He was a most earnest and successful worker, and was doing a great deal of good amongst the sailors and boat people. The chairman also spoke of the success which had attended Mr. Shaw's efforts, which be thought entitled him to the sympathy and support of all in the town. The programme was commenced by the fife band belonging to the mission, who very well played one of their selections. Recitations were given by Mrs. Rushton, Miss Higgins; Mr. James Yates, Mr. E. Higgins, and Master Burgess, who were listened to with very great pleasure, as I were also the songs, duets, and part-songs given by Mr. and Mrs. Jones, the Misses Jones, and Masters Jones. After an invitation from Mr. Shaw to the ladies present to assist in the sewing meetings for a bazaar and sale of which is shortly to be held, in aid of the proposed missionary house, and the usual votes of thanks, the meeting closed. On Wednesday evening, the teachers and friends of the mission presented to Mrs. J. J. Waterworth (late Miss Coleburn) a Bible and hymn book, as a token of their appreciation of her labours as a Sunday school teacher.

There is nothing more nourishing and warming in cold I weather than a cup of really good Cocoa, but (ha difficulty has been to obtain it pure. This may be secured at a cost of one halfpenny for a large breakfast cup by using Cadbury's Cocoa Essence, which goes three times as far as the adulterated and starchy compounds ordinarily sold, the smallest packet making fourteen breakfast cups of strong Cocoa.—ildrt.

SERMON ON LEFEOY ETA PATETOEN CLERGYMAN.-- On Sunday night, the Rev. William Preston, M.A.. of Holy Trinity Church, preached,.a sermon on the convict Lefroy.

PROPOSED MEETING OF FREEHOLDERS AT PrN'CORN.—On Wednesday next, a meeting of the freeholders of Runcorn will be held in the Commissioners' Board-room, at seven o'clock, to consider the recent enclosures of common land by several persons. Dr. Steele will preside. THE RuNrcont•r FREE LIBRARY MOVEMENT—AU influen- tially signed requisition has been presented to the chairman of the Runcorn Commissioners, in accordance with which a meeting of ratepayers will be held in the Bethesda school- room, Runcorn, on Monday, the .19th December, to decide whether a library shall be established in Runcorn. SERIOUS ACCIDENT AT WIDNES.—A man named Michael Doyle, of Victoria-street, Widnes, who is a labourer at Messrs. Roberts and Cooke's foundry, on Tuesday was carry- ing some iron castings from one part of the works to another when his foot slipped and he fell, the iron falling on him. He was stunned by the fall, and on examination his thigh was found to be fractured. He was at once taken to the Accident Hospital, and attended by Dr. McLennan. He is progressing favourably. RUNCORN SONS OF TEMPERANCE.—On Monday, the members of this order will have a grand field day. In the evening they will assemble at a quarter to seven, at Bethesda Congregational schoolroom, and headed lay the Weston Sons of Temperance band, will pdradethe town. At half-past seven a public meeting will be held in the schoolroom, under the presidency of Mr. Thomas Norman, and will be addressed by Mr. Malcolm Macleod, of Manchester. CHANGE RINGING at Itußcous.—Oa Saturday eight

members of St. Peter's pro-Cathedral Society of Change Ringers, Liverpool, visited Runcorn, and rang on the bells of All Saints' Parish Church a true peal of Kent treble bob major, containing 5,024 changes, in three hours fourteen minutes. The performers were :—Richard Williams, treble ; Henry Meadows, second; George Helsby, third; William Woods, fourth; Thomas Hammond, fifth • James Egerton, sixth ; Walter Littler, seventh ; and Robert - Williams, tenor. The peal was conducted by Robert Williams, and is the first complete peal of treble bob ever accomplished on these bells, although several attempts have been made by different societies.

WIDNES Parton CIIDECII SUNDAY SCDOOLS.—The ! members of the Young Men's Class have presented Mr. Imison with a beautiful album, specially manufactured, and containing the photographs of the .members. It bears the following inscription :—" To Mr. J. B. Imison Teacher and Friend. A token of esteem from the Widnes l'arish Church Young Men's Bible Class, Waterloo road School, 1881." During the month, also, the teachers at the branch Sunday School have presented to Miss Ifignett, who has resigned her class in consequence of family bereavement, a church service.

WIDNES AND TIIE FREE LIBRARIES' ACTS.-011 Tuesday evening, a largely attended meeting of ratepayers, called by Major Cross, the chairman of the Widnes Local Board, in reply to an extensively signed memorial, was held In the Volunteer Hall, of that town, to consider " The desirability of forming and having a Free Public Library in Widnes, Paid for out of a small rate." Major Cross presided, Mr. W. Kershaw, and Mr. Allen (clerk is the Local Board), also oc- cupied a seat on upon the platform. The Chairman, in open- ing the proceedingh said that on the 22nd ult., he received a requisition, signed liy more than ten ratepayers, asking him to call a public meeting to consider the question of whether the Public Libraries' Acts of 1853, 1366, 1871, and 1377 should be adopted by the township. They were, therefore, present that night either to give such a resolution their sanc- tion, or refuse to pass it. No one bat ratepayers who were actually on the list had a right to vote. Having made these observations, he would simply state that if sonic gentleman would move the adoption of the Act, he would proceed to business.—After a pause, the Chairman remarked that if no one would move the adoption of the Acts, he would simply put the resolution to the meeting in favour of the adoption of the Acts. He called those who were in favour to pass to the right hand side of the room, and those against it to walk to the left hand, so that he might count them easily.—This having been done, it was found that there were only eight out of the goodly number present in favour of the Acts being adopted in the town. The announcement was received with , loud cheers.—The Chairman: You clearly understand that those who are upon the left hand side of the room are against the adoption of the Acts. (Cries of " Yes," and ap- lolause.) I, therefore, declare that the public meeting as- sembled decides not to adopt the Free Libraries' Acts. (Ap- plause, and a voice : " Cock-a-doodle-do," and laughter.)— Mr. Briggs : Mr. Chairman, a respectable deputation waited upon the Local Board, and asked that the town might be derided into wards. The answer they got from you was that if the deputation would guarantee the expense incident to calling such a meeting, you would convene it. Now, I wish to know who is to be at the expense of calling the present meeting—the ratepayers or those who have signed the re- quisition Also, why you would call a meeting for this I particular purpose and not for the one about the town being divided into wards ?—The Chairman : In the C 390 of con- sidering whether the Free Libraries' Acts shall be adopted or not, the expenses have to be borne by the ratepayers, but in ' the case of a meeting to decide whether the township should be divided into wards or not, the expenses would have to be ' borne by the petitioners.—A voice: Were those petitioners ratepayers ?On the moticn of Mr. Briggs, a vote of thanks ' was passed to the chairinan for presiding, and carried with acclamation.—The Chairman suitably responded, after which the proceedings terminated. Crant AGAINST AN IRONFOUNDER BY A FORMER CORNIAN.—At the sitting of Wigan County Court, on Thurs- day week, before Mr. W.-W. Floukes, judge, Mr. John Yates , Mawson,(formerly of Runcorn), accountant and sharebooker, King street Wigan, sued to recover £5O from Mr. James Wright, ironfounder, carrying on business in the neighbour- hood of Wigan, the balance of a loan of £7O alleged to have been lent to the defendant.—Mr. Ellis appeared for the plaintiff, and Mr. Mulholland, barrister-at-law, for the de- fendant.—Mr. Ellis in his opening address, stated that f,r some years Mr. Mawson and the defendant had had business transactions together, Mr. Mawson acting both for the de- fendant and for his partners as auditor and assisting them with their books. Towards the end of 1879 and the beginning of 1881 the defendant and his partners had to find a con- siderable amount of money, Mr. Mawson was applied to for , his assistance. On the 7th July 1880, Mr. Mawsom lent Ito the defendant a sum of £7O, and at about the same time he negotiated a mortgage for that firm upon their worsk, thus enabling them to raise the amount they rcquired. The £7O was lent practically without any security, and'paiel to the defendant. Originally it was intended as a temporary loan, but as it was not paid back, Mr, Mawson asked the 0 - ' ' fendant to give him some securiiy for repayment, and the I , latter ultimately agreed that he. should deposit with Mr. Mawson some shares in a bank at Southport belonging to the defendant's daughters. These shares were of the nominal value of £5O. The defendant transferred these shares to Mr. Mawson, or his nominee, purely for the pampose of better securing the debt. Shortly after this, the bank got into difficulties, and the shares became worthless. Mr. Mawson saw Mr. Wright and pointed out to him the diffi- culty about the shares, and Mr Wright then assured him that not only would he pay the whole Of the £5O, the unpaid balance of the loan of £7O, but Mrs. should lose nothing in consequence of the shutting up of the bank. Mr. Mawson asked him for an I 0 U, but he said he should like a little time to consider, or something of that sort, and Mr. Mawson never got an I 0 U, or the money. In addition to this loan of £7O the firm had had the advantage of Mr. Mawson's ser- vices as auditor, and his feeswere not paid until Mr. Mawson took proceedings to recover £llB, including the balance of the loan. The defendants in the action paid into court £65, the amount admitted by the firm to be due, and an affidavit was made to tha effect that this £6O was not owing by the firml but was a matter between Mr. Mawson and Mr. Wright, and that the transfer was not made as a security at all, but in satisfaction of the debt of £5O that was at that time owing. . The question that the court would have now to decide was, whether the transfer Was in satisfaction of the debt of £5O, or whether it was merely a transfer for the purpose of securing payment of the debt to Mr. Mao-son by Mr. Wright. If there was an express agreement between parties that the transfer was only made as security there was an end of the defendant's contention. He might say that during the whole time the plaintiff held the.° shares up to the time of the transfer, they were never worth more than £4O, if they were worth that.—The case occupied a long time, and a large number of witnesses gave evidence.—ln summing up, His Honour remarked that it was quite clear the shares were originally placed in Mr. Mawson's hands for the purpose of being realised in order that he might be re- paid the £5O loan. Having before him so much conflict of testimony, lie must look at the case in this way. On the one side the Wrights were not pecple who were versed in stock exchange matters as well as Mr. Mawson was. Mr. Mawson knew what was the nature of these shares, and had better opportunities of judging what they might be worth than other people. At par they were worth £lOO, and Mr. Mawson, it might be, thought it would not be, a bad bargain to take them at £5O, the defendant tell ing him that whatever be got over he was to keep for himself. It seemed a remark- able thing that when there %vete two ways of transferring these shares, a right way and a wrong one; Mr. Mawson should adopt the wrong one. Looking at the document itself, and at the fact that Mr. Mawson had applied for new shares, he (the Judge) could come to no other conclusion than that he really did take the shares as payment for the loan, and he must, therefore, give judgement for the defend- ant with costs.

N PROVIDENCE ',CHAPEL, STOCKTON HEATH. - On Tnes- day evening a service of song, entitled "Eva," was given by the chapel choir, assisted by a few friends. In the absence of Mr. Bilsbrough, of Latchford, who had kindly promised to give the connective readings, but was unable to do so through indisposition, Mr. H. Eyes, of Appleton, read. Mr. J. Miller occupied the chair, and the harmonium was ably presided over by Mr. P. Harrison. The solos and duets were very well sung by Miss Richardson and Mrs. Clough, of Warrington, The solo in "Vital Spark of Heavenly Flame," by Harwood, was most effectively sung by Miss Richardson.

The Vicar of Frodsham lately invited Mr. Tomkinson, the Liberal candidate for the district, to speak on temper- ance at that town, and it is stated that he hhs also arranged with Mr W. S. Caine to give an address on the same sub- ject. This conduct has given rise to no small annoyance to the members of that party who, in former days, were said to have for their motto, "Beer and Bible." Perhaps the reverend gentleman is of the same opinion as Paul, Who thought it but a light matter to be condemned by any man's judgment, so long as he had the approval of his own con- science.

The annual church parade of the Runcorn Volunteers, will take place to-morrow (Sunday). Those who are living in hopes of dining at Christmas on the fatted goose or on sistecially fed poultry must now be particularly vigilant and use special means for the security of their winged property. About this time of the year mysterious disappearances of geese, ducks, and poultry become frequent. Men with thievish propensities, with a good knowledge of things and human nature in general and of farmyards and hencotes in particular, now prowl about in search of prey, and put a temporary stoppime to the plans for prospective Christmas dinners. Those who wish to keep up Christmas with clue- culinary accompaniments will take the hint.

The believers in purely denominational education in Runcorn are enlarging their school buildings, being evi- dently well convinced that there is very little chance of any serious competition in school matters, from the fact of the members of the School Board agreeing to spend money upon a school of an unsectarian character, at least under the present regime. Nearly every member has a personal interest in keeping competition out of the market, as they are connected as managers, or otherwise, with existing schools. Electing such gentlemen as School Board mem- bers, in the hope that they will make any gnat ado about putting up such noble schools as are to be found across the water, at Widnes, is about as wise as it would be for a co- operative society to place on the board of directors several of the largest shopkeepers in the town. I have nothing whatever to say in the way of criticism as to the abilities to deal with educational matters possessed by the present Board, as nearly every member is thoronghly conversant with such subjects, as long as the sleepy ratepayers are satisfied with their choice, and men can be found who arc willing to act as subscribers to funds for enlarging denominational schools—thus saving the town generally any serious ex- penditure—the present supineness of local educationalists will probably continue.
