DRUNK IN THE POLICE COURT. —For being guilty of this offence, on the 28th ult, Catherine McConn was fined 10s. and costs, or fourteen days' imprisonment. BRUTAL CONDUCT TO A. GOAT. A. middle aged man named Wm. Fitton, respectably dressed, wis charged with cruelly illtreatine a goat by inciting a dog to worry it.— Inspector Harper also proseculed in this case. The evidence was to the effect that defendant lodged at a beerlieuee c d led "The Pup," at Runcorn Hill, and on the 29t1r ult., the gut was put up to be raffled for, and won by a man named Pea- cock, who works at Weston. The winner did not wish to take the goat home the same night; and left it on the green belonging to the public-house, fastened to a stake in the ground by a rope. After the raffia defendant came to him and wanted him to sell the animal, but he would not. Later on a man named Bentlevweetout of the beerhousetand heard ' a screaming noise, something like a child crying. He founJ the defendant's dog worrying the goat. When asked what he was doing, he replied, "I was only trying my dog." The goat had subsequently to be killed.—Peacock was called, and said that on the morning after the raffle, defendant came to ask him how the goat was. He then followed defendant ' to a shed, when they found the animal lying, badly wounded in its forelegs, and not able to stand. They tried to get it up, but could not. The defendant told him that he tried to prevent the dog from worrying it. Ultimately the defendant bought the goat from him for 55., and took it away.— Frederick Bentley, labourer, said he went out of the beer- house after Fitton, and found the latter standing near the spot where the goat wee tied up. He heard the noise of a dog barking, and of a screaming sound such as a child might produce. He asked the defendant what was the matter, and he replied, "Oh! I am trying my dog on the goat." They then both tried to get the dog away, and ultimately suc- ceeded. Ile did not know whether Fitton was calling off the dog before he arrived on the scene.—Thom is Roberts, a labourer, living at Weston, said he occasionally acted as a butcher, and was called in by the defendant to kill the goat. lie found that one of its shoulders was dislocated, and one of its legs torn and bruised.—Defendant, in reply to ques- tions by the Bench, denied having incited the dog to bite the animal.—lle was fined 20s. and costs. SUNDAY DRINKING AT SUTTON. John Bailey, of the Aston Arms, Sutton, was summoned for having, on Sunday, the 20' le ult., sold liquor to persons who were not bona-fide travellers ; and aleo with having the premises open at im- proper hours.—Mr. W. 11. Linaker defended.—Sergeant Lowndes proved visiting the house, in company with P.C. Cooper, at ten o'clock in the morning, and in the taproom he found seven men, two of whom came from Weston, which was only about two miles distant. The landlady's daughter said the two men told her they came from Run- corm—Evidence was given by defendant, and his daughter Elizabeth Bailey, for the defence. The father maintained that people asking for liquor during prohibited hours on

FR ODSITA M. SHOPLIFTING AT FRODSTIAM BRIDGE. -On Tuesday evening two daring robberies were committed at Frodsharn Bridge, when the cellar of Mr. W. Walters, grocer, was entered by a ladder from the river side, and 3 hams, 251ber. of tobacco, 1 box of raisins, &c., taken therefrom; and on the same evening a leg of mutton and a quantity of beef were stolen from the premises of Mr. Bebbington, innkeeper, Frodsham Bridge. In the first instance, the robbery had been carefully planned, and was so successfully carried out that the goods were not missed until the following day. The p)lice have already obtained valuable information, and are thoroughly investigating the case.

POLICE CASES. IMONDAY.—Before E. A. Wright, Esq., and A. Thomas, Esq., ASSAULT.—John Littlemore, of Kingsley, was charged With assaulting his wife,: and was bound over to keep the Peace for six months, himself in £lO, and one surety in .£lO.

TIMRSDAY.—Before A. Thomas, Esq. ROGUE AND VAGABOND.—Joseph Forster was charged as a rogue and vagabond and frequenting a highway called Bridge-lane with intent to commit a felony.—Sergeant Johnson and P.C. Fowles proved the case, and the prisoner was committed for 14 days with hard labour. FElDAY.—Before E. A. Wright, Esq, and A. Thomas, Esq. STEALING LEAD.—Edward Antrobus was charged with I having, on or about the sth instant, stolen SSlbs. of lead of the value of 9s. 5d., the property of Mr. F. W. Dunsford, ' chemist, Frodsham.—The prisoner had been in the employ of Mr. Thomas Davies, who is extending a house belonging to Mr. Dunsford, and from information received by Sergeant Johnson, the prisoner was apprehended.—lie now pleaded guilty, and was committed for trial at Chester Quarter Sessions.

DISTRICT OF RUNJORN. THE PUBLIC LIB RARIES' ACTS, 18:55-1814-1871-1871. . [Received December 6th, 1881.3 To the Chairman and Memeers of the B mrd or Improvement Commissioners for the District of Runcorn. Whereas by an Act of Parliament passed in the 18th and 19th years of Queen Victoria, chapter 70, entituled The Public Libraries' Act, 1855, which Act was amended by another Act, passed in the 29th and 30th years of the reign of Queen Victoria, chapter 114. intituled " The Public Libraries' Amendment Act, 1866," it is provided that "The Board of any District being a place within the limits of any Improvement Act, shall up mi the Requisition In writing of at least ten persons assessed to, and paying the General District Rate, appoint a time not less than ten days nor more than twenty days from the time of receiving such Requisition for a Public Meeting of the persons assessed to, and paying such rate, in order to determine whether these Acts shall be adopted for such Districts, we, the undersigned, being persons assessed to, and paying Rees to the Improvement Commissioners for the District of Runcorn, do hereby respect- fully request you to call a Meeting of persons assessed to and paying Rates to your Board, for the purpose of determining whether or not the above mentioned Acts shall be adopted for such Districts, in manner provided by the said Acts. GREAT LIBERAL DIMONSTRATION AT WARRINGTON, On Wednesday evening last, Mr. J. G. MeMinutes, the deservedly popular member for the borough of Warring- ton, delivered his annual address to his constituents in the Public Hall, Warrington. The arrangements for the meet- ing were such as reflected credit on the energetic secretary of the Warrington Liberal Association, Mr. H. Roberts, and his brother, Mr. W. Roberts. The time announced fcr the com- mencement of the meeting was eight o'clock. Members of the ward committees were admitted by ticket to the gallery at 6-45, and at 7-15 all parts of the hall were opened to the I public, the result being that in about twenty minutes every part of the room was densely packed, whilst hundreds were obliged to go away, being unable to obtain admission. During the interval that elapsed from the time of ticket holders being admitted and the commencement of the meet- ing, Mr. F. R. Roberts presided at the organ, and played several popular tunes. Mr. George Wallington also sang the following popular new song, dedicated to the right hon. W. E. Gladstone, the audience joining in the claoru?, and Subsequently uniting with Mr. Wallington in singing it through : THE PILOT OF THE STATE. Sail on, thou peerless Argosy. Oh! Albion free and brave. And long may thy proud pinions float In triumph o'er the wave. ' Thy dauntless Pilot, firm as oak. Doth wa'ch Cie ebbing tide, He safely steers the gooi old ship, His glory and his pride. Cum:cos.—Sall, proudly sail! Freedom far and wide! He safely steers the good old ship, His glory and his pride. Old England hears the watchword now Her Pilot sounds afar, She trusts, in faith, to his firm band, Who steers by Truth's bright star. How gallantly he leads the van, And fears no hostile band, His crown of joy is England's fame, His own his native land. CAORUS.—SaiI proudly sAil Freedom far and wide! He safely steers the good old ship, His glory and his pride. And ye who stand enfranchised now, On this your wave wash'd soil, Give tribute to the Pilot bold, Ye noble sons of toil. For England still shall hold her sway, Old EL in boast a smile, And Scotia, blest, with commerce, crown Victoria's sea-gist Isle. CHOnna.—Sail, proudly sail! Freedom far and wide! He safely steers the good old ship, His glory and his pride. About a quarter to eight, seeing that no more persons could be admitted, it was resolved to commence the meeting, and the appearance of Mr. George Crosfield, the chairman, ac- companied by Mr. McMinnies, Mr. P. Rylands, Mr. J. Collings, and other prominent Liberals, was the signal for a great outburst of cheering, and the singing of" Auld lang syne." Mr. George Crosfield presided, and there were also on the platform Mr. J. G. McMinnies, M.P., Mr. Jesse Collings, M.P., Mr. Peter Rylands, M.P„ Alderman Holmes, J.P., Alderman Burgess, J.P„ Councillor John Crosfield, IP., Councillor Monks, J.P., Dr. Smith, J.P., Councillor E. Prominent on the centre of the platform in front of the , organ, were the figures 529, amid a profusion of flags, and ' around the galleries were the mottoes, County Franchise," "Free Trade," "God bless our worthy member," " Cheap Food," and "Land Law Reform," in white letters, on a green and red ground, so that the hall presented a very gay and festive appearance. The Cuanotax, who was received with cheers, said: Ladies and gentlemen,—ln the absence of your esteemed president, Mr. Rigby—(cheers)—who is on the Continent for the benefit of his health, I have either been requested or ordered, I scarcely know which—(laughter)—to take the chair on the present occasion. It is the first time since the election in April, 1880. that I have had the pleasure of meeting the Liberal electors, who so splendidly returned my friend, Mr. McMinnies—(loud cheers)—by a majority ex- ceeding all the majorities of all contested elections in Warrington since 1832. (Cheers.) I am, unfortunately, old enough to remember the election of 1832, and all the subsequent elections except the laet,when I was too nervous to De here, and the occasion of all others that I should haves liked to have been present. Warrington has had the privi- lege of returning a member of Parliament for 40 years, and during that 49 years the Liberal party have only bad it at all for eleven. The Tory party have had it for 38, and out - -of these '3B years we have, lam ashamed to say, allowed the •Conservative party to have it five times unopposed. ("They will have it no more," and loud cheering.) Your decisive majority in April, 1880, leads me to the conclusion that the probability i that for the next 38 years the Liberal party iu the borough of Warrington will have the privilege of return- ing one of their On opinion. (Loud cheers) It may be that we may have four or five unopposed elections. (Loud laughter.) lam not so sure that these are healthy things. I think a contested election a beneficial thing. (Hear' hear.) It educates people (hear, hear,) and you, in- creasing numbers and the increasing intelligence of the Warrington constituency has elevated Warring- ton to a. position that it will rank with even Burnley —(loud cheers)—and I think for the future that we may regard Warrington and Burnley as two of the safest and staunchest Liberal seats in Lancashire. (Loud cheers.) I said to you that your increasing numbers and increasing in- telligence which I am quite sure that you have has done this, bnt unlit also irLe electoral organisation in perfect order-- you must keep it In such order AS it was in April, 1880 ; you \ triust keep it in the order of a fire engine depot—such a one I as I saw in the United States in the spring of this year. I was walking with one of my colleagues through the city of Boston, and tire passed a tire engine depot. I said, "Mr. Bickemtaffe, we will go in here and see when they can get a fire engine out, and in what time." We went in and saw the superintendent, and told bins who we were.. He says, "Wait a minute; I will telegraph to the head office, and I will request him to send me a message that there is a fire in such a district." The telegraph bell sounded, I the horses that were at the back of the fire engine station trotted out of their own accord ; they came and placed themselves on each side of the pole, the harness fell down, the collar was buttoned. (Prolonged laughter and cheers.) In 15 seconds —I timed them with my watch—the horse and fire - engine were out of the place. (Hear, hear), Keep your electoral system in that way—(hear, hear)—wth our active friend, Mr. Roberts. (Hear, hear, and cheers.) When, he gets the telegraph message that there is a dissolution of Parliament; let him get the machinery out in 15 .rrinutes —(laughter)—let him have his canvas completed in 15 hours, and the election is over, and it will be over by the continuous return of a Liberal member of Parliament. (Hear, bear, and cheers.) I must not occupy your time further. You have several able speakers to address you, and your own very worthy member is the first one that is entitled to address you. (Loud cheers.) Mr. MoMINNIEs, M.P., on rising, was received with en- thusiastic cheers, and the song "For he's a jolly good fellow." Now I sometimes export iron to China. If I send that iron to Liverpool and it has cost me say LINO on board the ship that is the declared value of it, and the export is called £l,OOO, but I have to pay after that the freight, I, dock dues, expenses at Shanghai an. insurance which cost ' me £350. By the time that that iron gets to Shanghai, I must sell it for £1,350 if I am to get even interest upon my money without getting any profit. Well, my agent at Shanghai sells the iron and invests the proceeds in tea. and silk, and be ships them to this country. That shipment does not cost quite so much to me as the export of the iron did, but it does cost money, and for the same purpose that I told you it cost me £350 to send the iron out. When it arrives at London or Liverpool it has cost me £1,500, and without having any interest and without taking any profit I must sell it for £1,500 and it must be worth £1,500, and thus there is an import of £1,500 which pays for the export of £l,OOO. div.head: ernment Came into power, and it is improving.. Take my own trade.
div.p: ernment Came into power, and it is improving.. Take my own trade.
. - aL years ago half the looms and spindles in Lancashire em- ployed in the production of cotton goods were standing idle, and half of the rest .were working three and four days a
week. At the present time, it is no exaggeration to say-that there is not a loom or spindle idle in all Lancashire.

(Cheers.) Employment is p'lentifful ; wages have risen and they are likely to rise, and it is the same in reference to other trades Judged by what tests you like, notably by the traffic returns of the railways. (hear, hear.) These returns are increasing, as Mr. Gladstone said, "by leaps and bounds," and you may depend upon it that we are on the eve in fact, the period has arrived of a rapid and marked irnrovement in the trade of this country. Well, now, I have exhausted the time that I gave myself to speak, but I should like to say just half-a-dozen sentences about a very important personage in the politics of this town, and that is myself. Now the last Session of Parlia- ment, as my friends near me can tell you if they like, has been to advanced Liberals a time of great mental anxiety and great physical labour. • During that time I have, to the best of my judgment and ability, done my duty as your representative. '(:Lear, hear, and applause.) I have thought it more important to support the present Government than some of my colleagues below the gangway have thought it. I believe that, in my time at least, we shall never see a ' better Government than the present one. (hear, hear.) I bolieve that if we change we shall change for tho worse— (hear, hear)—and. if we had a Tory Government in power I believe it would be an evil thing for everyone of the three kingdoms. I ask you to judge of me and my course in Par- liament with consideration, forbearance, and patience. " Ihr -to say is this,

(Hear, hear.) Astor the future, what _ rave that in any position and in any capacity in which the Liberal party think that I can serve them my services are at their disposal. (Cheers.) At the same time I must say that the party which chooses for its leader and representa- tive an old man does not act wisely—(hear, hear)—and I look forward with pleasureable, and with even eager, satis- faction when I shall once more take my place with you in the ranks shoulder to shoulder in support of a younger and stronger man who hereafter shall carry the old flag to repeated victories. (Loud cheers.) Mr. JEssE Commlcs, M.P., said :—Mr. Chairman, ladies and gentlemen,-1 should like first of all to express my gratification at the singularly able and modest and dignified speech whi Ch we have just listened to. (Hear, hear.) When I I was asked to come down to Warrington I most gladly assented, for one reason, perhaps the chief reason, that I wished to show my respect to your member—(hear, hear)— respect which I may say, by his genial manners and sound Liberalism, he has won from all those wlip know him in the House of Commons. (Cheers.) As for his being an old man, my advice, needless advice, it appzars, to the men of Warrington, is to keep him as long AS you can—(hear, hear, and applause)--hecause I need only to look round at the mottoes to be reminded that there are great measures coming before Parliament, and those measures have for their object the upsetting of class interests for the benefit of the masses. (Cheers.) Therefore, I am-glad to see that in Warrington you have not chosen a class man—neither a soldier, nor a sailor, nor a landowner, nor a clergyman—(laughter)—and I wish every constituency would follov that example, because when these reforms come on it is unwise, you know, to set the cat to watch the cream. (Laughter and cheers.) Now, the work of Libsralism is the solution of some of the great problems which we have existing in our midst, the object is to find out the greatest meed of happiness for the greatest number. (Hear' hear.) That is is great a science as probably any other. Now, my friend, Mr. McMinnies, made a reference to what he called " thorough " Liberals. I have gr9t respect for moderate Liberals, those who some

- years ago were known as Whigs. They have done great work in their time—(hear, bear)—and I am no,t going to say one word against them. But their principles, and I believe they will almost admit it, are not suitable for the robust political reform of the present day. (iear, hear.) When I see them try to deal with to-day's problems they remind me of the American road described by the American humaurist, who says it is a very good road to begin with, and you think it is all right as to whither it leads; but it gradually narrows into a cart track, then dwindles into a squirrel rue, and leads up a tree. (Loud laughter.) Now, although we have to attack class systems, yet we must never forget our own dignity in doing so. Always remember we attack systems, but not men. (Hear, hear.) We, how- ever, are connected with A class quite as much as the men of whom I have spoken; but our weapons are education on the question we have before us, and then a quiet vote at the ballot box. Mr. McMinnies has given us some statistics as to the progress of the country.' You remember our great chief, Mr. Gladstone—(cheers)—said at Leeds that from 1842 to 1880, while the population had increased 53 per cent, the wealth of the country, judged by the income tax, had increased from £251,000,000 to £582,000,000,br more than doubled. (Cheers.) That is good; but there is a problem I wish to solve. How is it, with such an enormous increase of wealth, we are spending such enormous sums on the poverty and pauperism of this country? (Hear, hear.) How is it that in Birmingham we have one person in 33 a registered pauper? How is it that in the parish of Liverpool you have one person out of 33 in the same condition? Go further. Mr. Caird has told us that in 20 years the capitalised value of the land of England has increased by 331,000,000 of money. An eminent authority a few weeks ago told us that in 24 years, from 1852 to 1876, the rentals of the English estates had increased by ten and a half millions, which, at 25 years' purchase, would represent the value of the land in 1876 as worth 250 millions more than it was in 1852. That is satisfactory, but again, I ask how is it that onr agricultural labourers in all the .eouthern and midland counties of England are at this moment living, or trying to live, on 10s. a week? ("Shame.") That is a problem affecting a very numerous class, and they must be considered. (Hear, hear.) Mr. McMinnies said that so many years ago men were living in Bolton on only Is. 3d. per head per week. What we said Iwas that their policy aggravated the bad trade, and we said' that the policy of disturbance in Europe was certain to lead to perplexity and disturbance in trades at home. (Hear, hear.) The fact is that the Tory speakers never seem to be able to understand that the country out of London at the beginning of last year was determined to get rid of the very worst Government that ever governed this country. (Ap- plause.) Mr. Cross attributed the result of the election in April, 1880, to Mr. Gladstone's wild speeches in Midlothian. Well, those may have been wild speeches, and they may have bad some effect upon the general election, but I should not be at all surprised if they had more effect upon the country than certain tame speeches that we have heard in Seuth-West Lancashire within the last few months. (Laugh- ter.) The fact was that the country had made up its mind before Mr. Gladstone spoke in Midlothian that it would dis- possess the Government in power, and while we never did attribute all the bad trade to the Beaconsfield Government, we did say, and we do say, that the .. . .

land? The proceeds from our farms and our homesteads are not less than from 250 millions to 300 millions sterling per annum. That is a large sum. It is more than _all our ex- ports pat together, and if we may take the word of Earl Leicester, Mr. Lawes, and others, that -amount may be in- creased by at least 100 millions. .Now if you take all our experts to Russia' France, Germany, Belgium, Australia, and New Zealand you will find they do not amount to 100 millions sterling, and yet we are losing that sum through the bad system of agriculture. As to the remedy for this sate of things, some of the gentlemen re- ferred to by Mr. MeMinnies seem to think that we .only want fine weather and a change of Government and then we shall be all right. Other men would have Reciprocity and Protection; but, while all this is going on, who among them ever refers to the loss, the gradual loss, of that best of markets which lies at our own door'? it to the unborn --- age. You may go still further. A man can burden the land with all sorts of settlements,—charges for widows and wives, annuities, marriage dowries, and mortgages, payments to buy a commission for this nephew and to educate at relative, and a hundred other different burdens. The con- sequence is that you hardly ever get a real owner of landed property in England. A man may be a spendthrift and a bankrupt, but still he has a life interest in the land, and cannot get rid of it. That is what we understand by the powers of the dead hand—that is to say, a man who may have been lying in his grave for years is now managing to a great extent a large portion of the land of England. Well, this is entail and settlement, a law plain enough to under- stand, but as foolish as anything can be. Then there is the transfer of laud, a process the most uncertain, costly, and dilatory. I should take up too much time to tell you what makes the transfer of land so expensive. (Clio of "Go on.") Suffice it to say that you have to employ lawyers of the highest talent, and we know thatthey must be paid. I will give you an instance. Two or three years ago there were three acres of land bought, and £l5 tithe rent charge, and the legal expenses on that, and it is not a rare case by any means, amounted to £ll7. (Laughter.) What is the consequence of all this? The old yeomen of England have died out, that is to say, they have been bought out, for the enormous powers . . .

_ given to the landowners have been an inducement to cer- tain wealthy men to acquire land at any price. The result is that in England, which comprises 38 millions of acres, we find four millions of acres are possessed by 100 men, ten millions, or one-fourth of the land, is 'possessed by under 1,000 persons. (" Shame.") Probably less than one-half the number of persons in this hall possess one-fourth of England. (A voice: " We are only lodgers, here." Laugh- ter.) If you go into Scotland you will find one-fourth of the whole country owned by 12 men. I could not tell you the powers which these men who own most of the land possess. They have all the power of the House of Lords, and a great deal of power—too much—in the House of Com- mons; but I could not tell ' you what powers they have secured for themselves. Yea know they claim under the game laws the wild beasts, the wild fowls, and the fish in the rivers; and there are lots of claims which those who live in towns scarcely know of. How many of you, for instance, know of the rights of heriot?—which means that if a small freeholder dies the lord of the manor may come and take the very best anim3l in the possession of the widow by right. ("Shame.") Failing an animal, he may take the best article of furniture. "Oh," but you say, "that is not put into force." But it is. I know a -case—many, in fact:— where a short time ago a landlord, who pos- sessed 35,000 acres, sent his agent, on the death of a small freeholder of four acres, who claimed and took away the only horse the widow possessed. ("Shame.") The widow had to redeem it as she was at. lowed to do by paying two-thirds its value, and she paid £l4. ("Shame.") I know another case in which a poor family had no horse, and the agent took the looking-glass from the mantel piece. I know another in which the agent went and finding nothing in the house worth taking but a very poor clock, took that down, but it was not worth taking away. (A voice: "Boycot him.") I mention these things to show you some of the enormous powers which landlords have preserved for themselves. I might tell you about the manner in which the commons of England have been taken by certain men who would find it difficult to

supported more than the landlord class. These are wise words, for it is not safe for so few people to possess the land of England. /Hear. hear.) the political economist of the State advancing inoney to labourers and others. Now, if it were a question between man and man, I should agree with that objection. But it . .
, is right, I hold, as a matter of public interest, and as a luestion affecting the property of the country generally. . . . . .

. . . Besides, it has been accomplished by the Irish Land alit, by which a tenant is enabled to acquire possession of a farm, the State advancing three-fourths of the purchase money. In Ireland, landlords have been lent money by the State at one per cent; and at the time of the corn • laws the State lent—or rather they lent themselves, so that it was the same thing—money to. be repaid by 22 annual instalments. Most of them laid that money out in improvements on which they charged their tenants a very considerable interest--(hear, hear)—so that what is good for political economy in the case Of the landlord, is surely in accordance with political economy in the case of the labourer. (Hear, hear.) At least I cannot see any difference. Our great friend Mr. Bright—(cheers)—when speaking of the Land Bill of Ireland, talked of putting the labourers to cultivate the waste land of Ireland. He asked what are one, three, or five, or ten millions for such a purpose ?—(hear, hear)—and I say if you can bring the people back on the land in England, and make ten people live where one is now, what ara one, three, or five, or ten millions to try the experiment? Why, we spent 23 millions of money in the Afghan war—(" shame")—for • a scientific frontier— (derisive laughter)—which no man ever saw or ever will see. (Hear, hear.) That sum would have given half an acre of good agricultural land to every labourer in this kingdom. (Hear, hear.) But another objection -”-lends —.mid go to these poor

is that -the money-lenders wou,- go to 1a..... people, and they would soon be sold out. My answer to that is, these men should not mortgage thejand or be allowed to do so, and that would dispose of that difficulty. They should not sublet the land either, but as soon as they could no longer till it, they should be at liberty to sell it. Then I have to remind you 'that such a system would nearly, if net quite, abolish, that great difficulty and disgrace of pauperism. (Hear, hear.) Here is an extract of what Mr. Thornton, who is a great authority on this subject, says,— "As long as the connexion of the peasantry with the land remained unbroken, England was perfectly free from every symptom of pauperism, and the supply of labour instead of exceeding the demand was so deficient as to induce Parlia- ment to interfere to keep down its price. But almost imme- diately after the consolidation of small farms commenced, legislation took a different turn." I say that every man in this town, when he draws a cheque for the payment of the poor's rate, has a right to say "that is my contribution to the English landlordism ;" because the people from the coun- try are forced into our towns where they cause a surplus of labour, and at the sane time a diminution of trade. (Hear, hear.) Let any clerk who is in a situation for a small salary ask how many have been sons of people connected with the land, let every workman remember the •men'who had been forced into the towns, and let the shopkeeper remember that this competition in trade is catS d by competition on the part of men, a percentage of whom would be on the land making trade instead of competing with those in trade. I will not keep you any longer. I must thank you for the manner in which you have listensd to these hurried remarks, which you must bear in mind defend not confiscation. I have attended as many met tines of workingmen as nost n and I say with pride I never heard a single dishonest act in public policy ever advocated by the workingmen of this country. (Cheers. But I would exhort you when you see the newspapers filled with tenant rights and landlord rights, always to assert there are such rights as labour rights as well —(hear, hear) ;—and you will be able to secure those rights by first understanding the question, and then by your en-

tbusiasm at the ballot box. Lien I would say it Word for those poor unfortunate men in the counties who have no votes, who are at this moment the pariahs of political society who look to you, whose cause you never find in any newspaper, whose condition is only known to those who have been among them as I have been among them during the past few months. You find them rising when the stars are out, and going out to work ankle deep at ditching, some- times coming home at night with their bread, and very little else, and then getting up next morning, putting on the damp clothes and going on from morn to night until the seasons seem one dreadful grind of human toil. lan now speaking of tens ,of thousands of your fellow workmen. After all thi sploughing and mowing when the labourers' backs are bent and their knees are weak they work up to the very eve of life, up to the closest proximity of the grave, because they know that if they stop the horrid workhouse is their lot. ("Shame.") This is no fancy picture I am drawing, but one to be seen in the bulk of the agricultural counties of the Country. When he fails at last he goes into the House, and then he appears before those persons who are called the Guardians, but very soon he finishes up and his death is reported to the Board. Then the parish bell is tolled, and he is put by the parish grave digger in the six feet of earth, which is the only portion that the agricultural labourer of this country can ever hope to possess. ("Shame.") That is the law. But if you workingmen of the towns who have votes yourselves, and who have better objects yourselves, can forsake these tens of thousands and hundreds of thousands of men, I say you are not true to your order. (Hear, hear.) You am not true to those who are in the condition you were in years ago, and thus I would advise you to understand this question for your own sakes and for that of others. I would ask every political economist to pause with me for a moment, and reckon up the aggregate earnings of a poor labourer in the course of his long life, and then see whether he has had his share. As my friend Mr. Rylands knows, when anything comes up in the House of Commons affecting the army, you have the soldiers down to a man; when you have anything coming up affecting the Church, you have the ecclesiastical section watching with the utmost eagerness. Likewise if there be a word said touching the land, every man interested is alive. blow, when we attempt to settle the land question will the Arkingmen be as true to their order us other classes are true to their's. , -- show their right to them. (Hear, hear.) But the most serious thing of all is that the produce of the land which affects he people more than anything else has decreased to such an extent that the land of England is producing only Iwo-thirds of what it ought to produce. In every census in England we find that our country districts are becoming more and more silent. Where do the people go? . They go into the towns to compete with you in you; labour, and thus lessen your wages—(hear, hear)—instead of remaining on the land, prodpcing wealth, and beconfing customers to the towns. (Cheers.) -Wow, I have spoken about the labourers. They have, as I said,los. a week. I sat down in a cottage some weeks ago where a man was supping from his bread and onions, whick was all he could get. That man had 10s. a week. Along side-of him; living in the same parish, there was a landowner who had a tract of land stretching ten miles ahead and four miles wide—(" Shame ")—much of which at this moment is lying on his hands scarcely culti- vated. So that you see on the one hand we have the labourer willing to cultivate, and on the other the land uncultivated. Now, the Farmers' Alliance, as you, are aware, are endeav- ouring to alter this state of affairs, and they are about to bring in a Bill to give compensation to the farmer for tines- hausted improvements, and to allow him to sell those im- provements in the open market. (Hear, hear, and cheer's.) Well, that is do' good, but it does not go far enough to my mind. I do not like bit-by-bit legislation. It stops the way very often of more complete measures. Besides that, the labourer is left out of sight altogether. I wrote to the Farmers' Alliance and begged of them to take the cause of the labourer into their scheme, but the reply I received was that he was outside the scope of the present measure. I have been a great deal among the labourers, and I have al- ways known them to be Outside the scor of every measure. (Cheers.) What I want you to admit is this—that land is different to any other property in this respect. It must be employed to support the people. (Hear, hear.) If you get mills erected in this part of the country, and people don't choose to work them, other men will build mills, and the community does not suffer, and if a m in •chooses to destroy his personal property the community does not suffer. But if he claims to lay in the seed of half the country and destroy it, the people have a right to say "No;" and if he claims, as he did in Scotland, to clear thousands of poor creatures off the land, in order that deer might be kept for the sport and amusement of a few persons, the people have a right to say, "No; we will not allow it." me sty, is the bond that should bind the English and the Irish of this town. Are you English workipgmen generous enough to the Irish? D 3 you ever consider that there would not have been an Irishman in Warrington or in England had he not been forced out of his own country? (Cheers.) When you look at an Irishman you should be moved with pity and sympathy for him. (Hear, hear.) Are you mean enough to say that he is idle? • Would you not be idle if on the Saturday night, after your wages were put on the table someone came and swept the bulk of them away? You say he is ignorant: Do you remember that the laws made it a felony to teach him the multiplication table? Is he idle in other countries? Is he idle here? The English working man who turns his back on his Irish fellow does a mean act. He does not remember the history of that which has driven him here, and the great debt which, as a natior, we owe to him. (Cheers.) Therefore, let this be a bond of union. His cause, the cuase of land and labour, is your cause, for there will come a time when trade will not be so good again, and if our land decreases we shall have nought to put in. its place. I know that the Sandonq, the Argylls, and the Salisburys will unite against such reform, but if . the struggle' must be between landlords and the people, let that struggle crftne. (Cheers.) Why, look _ .

„ at Ireland. Forty odd years ago there was a Royal Commis- sion which reported that the great evil of Ireland arose from the fact that the tenants' improvements were robbed by the landlords' exactions for rent—(hear, hear,)—and from that time to this there had been men in Parliament and out of Parliament denouncing the exactions of the landlord, and saying that the fruits of the tenants' industry were being stolen. He recollected that he need to vote in the House of Commons with his late friend Mr. Isaac Butt—a man for whom he had the greatest regard and affection—in favour of that gentleman's bill advocating nxity of tenure; and after he (the speaker) came out of the lobby his Tory and Whig friends used to say, ” What have you been doing? Trying to rob the landlords of their property? We hope that you will not vote to rob us of our property." (Laughter.) The Land Act which Parliament had passed was a very much greater measure than Mr. Butt had any idea of bringing before the members of the House of Commons • but let them mark this fact, that forty years made a great alteration. If ' during the time of the Royal Commission the land question had been dealt with by the Legislature the probability was that we should have had a prosperous Ireland to-day; but the proposed reforms were resisted by the landed interest, and the consequence was tha during forty years there had been exactions made upon the tenants of Ireland, who had been pressed deeper and deeper down into distress and star- vation; and then when these poor wretched tenants had been unable to pay these exorbitant rents, the terrible evic- tions of which they had so often read had followed, sweeping the side of the country bars, and sending the tenants to the workhouse or the gaol. Let them have some consideration for these fellow-countrymen of theirs—he called them fellow- countrymen—in Ireland; and remember • that, they, as Englishmen, had been so long a time in giving justice to the tenantry of the sister isle. He was afraid they would have a great struggle on this question in.Engltnd. Irmight be that in the agricultural districts there would be great suffering before these reforms were carried, out, but they could not be delayed for ever, as the competition of foreign . .

countries was so influencing the matter that it must be taken into consideration. He hoped that by the intelligent suppott of the people out of doors they would be enabled to secure measures in the House of Commons which would be for the good of the masses at large. He should not, as he had previously remarked, exhaust their patience by any extended observations, after the very able speech of his friend the .member for the borough„ and his honourable friend who sat near him (the speaker). He had, however, a most pleasing duty to perform, and that was to mote the following resolution :—" That this meeting desires to tender its heartiest thanks to John Gordon McMinnies, Esq., M.P., for the manner in which he has performed his duties during the past sessions of Parliament, and at the same time expresses its unabated confidence in him as the representa- tive of the borough, and its determination to use every possible legitimate means to retain the present proud posi- tion of the Liberal party in Warrington." He had, how- ever, been at a great many political meetings in Warrington, but he was never at one which was superior to that he had then the honour of addressing. Let them look at tha character of that meeting. He knew the character of many of those who had the honour to compose the gathering, and it represented the cream of the constituency of Warrington. He was delighted, as he felt sure they all were, to see his friend Mr. Geo. Crosfield in the chair. (Applause.) He was also delighted to see on that platform and in the hall so many earnest Liberals; and exceedingly gratified to think the Liberal party in the borough when they selected his friend Mr. McMinnies as a representative of Warrington chose a man of mature and thorough political opinions. (A Voice : A thorough Radical. Applause.) There *as one thing which he would say about his• friend Mr. McMinnies—he had never been at a university, he was not a master of arts, or even a bachelor of arts. (Laughter.) He could recollezt duriag his dine when it used to he said that in order to make "Ban a good member of Parliament, he ought to have a collegiate career and a university degree. Well, he did not by any means despise those qualifications, but they bad now-a-days very much higher schools of political education than they had a number of years ago. They had now a means of political education by a cheap press ;—they had opportunities of knowing what was going on all over the world; and he could answer for this, that long before some of the young aspirants for, university degrees were born, his friend Mr. McMiunies was working hard in political matters, and was obtaining political experience.. Although his friend . . _

might not be master of arts, afar as a universitY degree was concerned, he took a very good Radical degree notwith- standing ;—he had that kind of education which they wanted In the House of Commons. They wanted 'men in Parliament who had been identified with the people of this country, and with the great movements which had caused its rapid advance in the scale of nations, and who would be firm enough in St. Stephen's to support principles which would be for the benefit of the people at large. (Applause.) There was, nevertheless, one point in the speech made ley Mr. MeMinnies with which he did not agree, and he was sure the audience did not coincide with him (Mr. McMinnies) in regard to it either. Their borough member talked as if he was an old man. Well, they did not believe in old men in the House of Commons at the years of Mr. McMinnies. (Applause and laughter.) In fact that gentleman might be described as rather a promising young legislator. (Applause and much laughter). The fact was that Lord Palmerston was Prime Minister of England at a very much greater age than Mr. McMinnies. (Renewed laughter.) He dare say many of those present had been in the House of Commons, and looked down from the gallery, on doing which, if the House was very full, they must have been struck with one remarkable fact, viz , that in all the assemblies in which they had been they never saw so twiny bad heads. (Great laughter and cheers.) They did not believe that Mr. McMinnies was old at all ;—he-was young and vigorous in their service; and in proposing that resolution he did not do so with the idea that the member for the borough was going to withdraw after he had served the present Varliament. (Hear, hear and loud applause.) No, Mr. McMinnies would not withdraw ;—certainly not; but when they wanted him to fight he would ba found there. Talking of age, he understood that there was a very matured gentleman at Walton Hall, ready for the fight. (Laughter.) Well, now, if they might call them old cocks, and they were to fight, he would back his old friend Mr. McMirries, who was sitting by his side to win. . .

(Great laughter and applause, amidst which the speaker resumed his seat.> . • Mr. F. A. ROBERTS rose with great pleasure to formally second the resolution. It had been said that night that Mr. McMinnies had been returned by a tremendous majority ; greater than any within the last 30 years ; and it was said at the time of the election that he would wisely and ably represent: them in the Rouse of Commons. NOW, he remembered that occurrence when he was asked to second the resolutton, and trusted he might be present at that.meet- ing to assure Mr. McMinnies that their confidence had not diminished but had rather increased. If it turned out that their Conservative friends liked to show fight again, he felt convinced that the 500 majority would be again secured. Mr. FLOOD said that not many days ago one of his Tory friends said to him in a very serious manner, " Mr. Flood, I am afraid you have made a great mistake, at least your party have in returning a Liberal member for Warrington." Well. he did think a mistake had been made when they were 37 years without a Liberal member. The question might be asked by their good friends the enemies, how it was that they placed so much, confidence in their member; and when he saw ' men as the Crosfields and

.te saw upon that platform BlM- the Armitages, the answer was that the man of their choice tellech was worthy of the choice of the whole constituency. He represe found that the majority of the constituencies throughout the all I n kingdom were what they might call Radical members. They sist—n were anxious at the last election that the opinion of the from il nation should be heard in the House of their Legislators; and moth that the voice of the majority might be at yo heard, and that Liberalism might be predominant throughout Thi,

A
RUNCORN BOARD OF COMMIS- SIONERS.

The monthly meeting was held on Monday. There were l present Messrs: Steel (in the chair), Norman, Lyon, Mc- Dougall, Whittaker, P. Speakman, Briscoe, Shaw, Handley, Lake, Hazlehurst, Meadowcroft, J. J. Speakman, Linaker (law clerk), Brookes' (secretary), Mouritz (medical officer), Barker (surveyor). MEDICAL OFFICER'S REPORT. Dr. 31013RITS reported that the number of deaths registered in Runcorn during the month was 24. One death had also occurred at Halton, making the total number of deaths 25. Of these ten were due to pulmonary complaints, four to abdominal complaints, four to brain affections, four to senile decay, and two to jaundice. Scarlatina and premature birth accounted one each, representing a death rate of 20 per 1,000 per annum. Eleven deaths had occurred amongst children of three years old and under, and eight under one year. One inquest had been held. MR. BEASLEY stEs TUB BOARD FOR £3,000 DAMAGES. The CECAIRMAN said a notice had been received from Mr.l Thomas Beasley (formerly of Runcorn, and now øf Over- ton) by Mr. W. H. Linaker (clerk), Mr. Win. Brookes (the secretary), Mr. John Parry (nuisance inspector.), and by each member of the Board, stating that according to the form of the statute in such case provided, he gave them notice that he should, after the expiration of one month, cause a writ of summons to be issued out of the queen's Bench Division of Her Majesty's High Court of Justice, for having, on the 3rd of July last and other days, falsely and maliciously written and published of and concerning him a certain re-solution falsely stating he had stolen, or was in possession of, certain property belonging to the Commis- sioners, which had been stolen, and directing a criminal prosecution against him in respect of the said offence. And that some of them, on the 3rd July and upon other days, had falsely and maliciously spoken and published concein- ng him certain statements charging him with having stolen or been in possession of ttie said property, and that he had fraudulently removed his goods from Waterloo House in Runcorn to evade payment of his rent, whereby he had heen injured in his profession and character. Also, that on or about the 4th July they wrongfully, maliciously, and with- out reasonable or probable cau-e, did apply, or cause appli- cation to be made, to the Clerk to the Juctices for the Run- corn division, for a summons or warrant against him, falsely charging that he did feloniously steal certain goods and chattels alleged to be the property of the Commission- ers, and falsely charging that he had stolen certain fixtures alleged to be their property. Also, that they had procured Mr. C. W. Hazlehurst, J.P., to grant such warrant. Also, that on the 6tla July they did break and enter, and remain for a long time in possession of the said dwelling-house in Mr. Beasley's occupation. For this Mr. Beasley claimed £3,000 damages. The communication was dated the 2nd inst.; and had also been served upon Mr. C. W. Hazle- hurst, J.P. Mr. HANDLEY suggested that the notice should be taken

as read. The CHAIRMAN then suggested that it might be a pru- dent course to refer the notice to the Highway and Sanitary Committee. The CLERK: There is nothing to refer to them. He simply gives you notice that at the expiration of a certain time he intends to take proceedings. The discussion then dropped. ALLEGED SERIOUS NUISANCE FROM THE GLYCERINE WORKS. The following (copy) letter was read :—" White-street, Runcorn, 3rd December, 1881.—Dear Sir,—! heg to call your attention to the noxious vapours arising from the Glycerine Works, which is something abominable, both night and day. I have made several complaints to the manager, and he promised that it should not occur again ; but it keeps going worse. My tenants, when the wind comes towards my pro- perty, are complaining daily that the vapour makes them sick, and ro affects them that they cannot eat their food. I bad to call in the doctor to my wife and child. I enclose copies of complaints, from which you will sae that unless the nuisance is abated I shall have all my tenants leaving their houses, which will be a very yerious matter to me. I have avoided troubling you until now, as I had hoped the nuisance would have been abated. Yours truly, HENRY WHITE. P. 8.—1 had a complaint from one of my tenants on Saturday morning, stating that his family were nearly suffocated on the Friday night." The CHAIRMAN observed that the Secretary had written to the proprietor of the Glycerine Works on the subject, and had received the following note in reply :—" Rnncorn, Dec. Ist, 1881.—Dear Sir,—Please excuse my not replying until now to your communication of November 18th. I request you to kindly assure the Commissioners, for my part, that everything shall be done, and special care taken so that no unpleasantness, or nuisance, is caused to the inhabitants by our works. I am, yours respectfully, A. Semsomm, manager of the Glycerine Works." Mr. PHILIP SPEARMAN said he had been to the top of Mill Brow to test the matter personally, and whilst he was there he certainly did not feel any particular smell. It was a very serious matter indeed to harrass works which had just been introduced into the town, and they ought to be careful that it was not done unnecessarily. Mr. SHAW moved, and Mr. WILLIAMS seconded, a motion in favour of the Inspector of Nuisances enquiring carefully into the alleged complaints, and then reporticg to the

Board. Dr. MCDOUGALL considered that the two questions for enquiry were, first, whether the vapour from the works was a nuisance, and secondly, whether it was injurieus to health. The Inspector of Nuisances could not be considered an authority on such questions, and the matter ought to be placed in the hands of the Medical Officer. Mr. Normax The Inspector can draw the attention of the Medical Officer to it. Mr. LAKE was of opinion that the question of health had really nothing whatever to do with the case, as the Boar6l had power to take steps if a nuisance were proved to exist, whether it was injurious to health or not. The motion was then put and carried. THE LOCAL GOVERNMENT BOARD AND THE NEW BYE-LAWS. The SECRETARY read the following letter :—" Local Go- vernment Board, Whitehall, S.W., 25th November, 1881.— Sir,—I am directed by the Local Government Board to acknowledge the receipt of your letter of the 14th instant, forwarding a, printed copy of bye-laws proposed to be made by the Improvement Commissioners for the district of Run- corn with respect to new streets and buildings. The Board return the printed copy herewith, and at the same time direct mo to state that they have examined the proposed clauses, and that they find that, with few exceptions, the clauses are open to objection on various grounds. Under these circumstances, the Board suggest that the Commis- sioners should abandon the proposed clauses in favour of a selection based wholly on the model clauses. Assuming that the Commissioners will be prepared to adopt this course, the Board forwar lherewith, f h Or e use of the Com- missioners, a draft form of series four of the model bye-lawS. The Board enclose, for the consideration of the Commis- sioners, the accompanying copy of a letter which the Board has received from Mr. G. F. Smith, agent to the Bridgewater and Ellesmere Trustees, in reference to the proposed bye- laws.-1 am, sir, your obedient servant, J. F. Rams, assis- tant secretary." After some remarks from Mr. Handley, the letter was re- ferred to the Bye-Laws Committee, on the motion of Mr. SHAW, seconded by Mr. P. SPEAKMAN. The plans of the Bridgewater Navigation Co. were also passed, on the proposition of Mr. P. SPEAKMAN, seconded by Mr. NORMAN. SANITARY MATTERS.—THE FOUNTAIN WATER. The MEDICAL OFFICER and Mr. BARKER (surveyor) had presented a report to the Highway and Sanitary Committee, from which we abstract the following :—" We inspected the Camden soap works, and devoted a considerable time in examining the process of delivery from these works to the glycerine works. We ascer- tained that the soap lees were driven by force of steam power from a large egg-ended boiler through a hori- zontal iron pipe 3in. diameter, about 17f1. high, and after passing through the walls descended by its own gravity 400 yards along the canal bank to the glycerine works, through 4in. iron pipes laid underground, and ultimately deposited into a large tank, which is constructed of brickwork and cement, and is about Bfl. below the surface of the ground. After some further process the said liquor is passed into another tank, also constructed of brickwork and cement, and which is also below the surface, an old sawpit being utilized for this one. We have been able to ascertain that some six weeks ago an accident occurred, causing a leakage in the bottom of the last-named tank, resulting in the loss of a con- siderable portion of its contents ; and we have no doubt that this found its way through the made ground into the culvert stream, thus polluting the water in its course to the fountain. We may state that we bad the assurance of the manager (Mr. Sansom) that every precaution had been and would be taken to prevent any recurrence of similar mishaps." The committee recommended that the Law Clerk be in- structed to write to Mr. G. L. Smith with reference to the transfer of land for the Bridge Slope, and also to the solici- tors to the railway company, asking to be furnished with an estimate of the cost of putting in force their powers for the compulsory purchase of the said land.—Mr. NORMAN moved and Mr. P. SPEAKMAN seconded the motion for the adoption of the minutes, which was passed. PORTLAND AND CAWDOR STREErS. It was resolved, on the motion of Mr. HaztEurns-e, seconded by Mr. SHAW, that the owners of property in these streets should be called upon to complete them at once.

WARRINGTON TOWN COUNCIL. A special meeting of the Council was held in the Council chamber at the Town Hall, on Tuesd ey evening, in pursuance of the Elementary Education (Industrial Schools)Act, 1879, to consider the making of a contribution towards the mainten- ance, in a certified industrial School, of the several boys named in the minutes of the School Attendance Committee ordered by the magistrates to be sent to such certified industrial school. The Mayor (Alderman Pickmere) presided, and there were also present Aldermen Holmes, Webster, Harrison, Kean, Davies ; Councillors Milner, Platt. Woolfall, Taylor, Ashton, Wallington, Barker, Monks, Caldwell, Mackie, Jeans, Burgess; Messrs. W. H. Brook (town clerk), J. L. Whittle (deputy town clerk), C. Chorley (borough treasurer). Alderman WEBSTER moved the usual resolutions, which were seconded by Alderman HARRISON, and carried. Alderman WEBSTER. replying to Councillor Monks, said the sending of these boys to industrial schools was now getting a very serious thing, and he hoped the magistrates who were on the Bench would see that the parents were made to pay a proper sum towards the maintenance of their children. The cost to the Council was about 28. 6d. per week for each of the nine children now in industrial schools. Replying to Mr. Milner, the Alderman said the children were sent to the industrial schools by the magistrates, and not by the Committee. THE MONTHLY MEETING. The monthly meeting was afterwards held, and besides the members above named there were present Councillors Dixon, Francomb, Sutton, Brown Litton, Rid gway, Pier- point, and Crosfield ; and Mr. T. Lc:ngdin (borough surveyor). THE LIVERPOOL UNIVERSITY COLLEGE. The MAYOR skid he had received a letter from Mr. W. J. Stewart, bon, secretary of the University College, Liverpool, informing him that in accordance with the charter of the ' University the Warrington Council had power to appoint 1, one governor of the University, who would hold office for five years, or until death or resignation. The gentleman elected need not be a member of the Council. His Worship added that Mr. William Beamont, an old and valued friend, not only of the Corporation, but of the town, would be a very suitable person for the Corporation to nominate as governor from Warrington. He could not formally move the resolu- tion that night, but should be glad to hear an expression of opinion. Alderman DAVIES said theycould not pay a more graceful tribute to Mr. Beamont, lookidk at his literary position and his connection with Warrington. He was worthy of all the honour they could give him on such a board. Alderman HOLMES thought if there was an inhabitant of Warrington wor hy of the honour it was Mr. Beamont. He was the first Mayor, and no man had done so much to make Warrington known throughout the land. Aldermen WEBSTER said Mr. Beamont's great knowledge and character made him quite worthy of any honour they could confer upon him. The MAYOR remarked that he had asked Mr. Beamont if he would undertake the office if he was proposed, and he had received the following letter Dear Mr. Mayor, I return the papers relating to the Liverpool University College, which you so kindly sent me. I have read through the Royal Commission, the clearness of which will bear an advantageous comparison with any earlier document of the same kind. lam flattered by you thinking me fit to be one of the life governors, the responsibilities of which, divided by so numerous a body, cannot bs very onerous, and it it should be the wish of yourself and Town Council, with whom the appointment rests, I still feel it my duty to obey. At the same time I shall feel no jealousy if any other gentle- man, of whom there are many more worthy, shall be fixed upon for this honoUrable office.—l remain, yours very truly, W. BEAMONT." The Council were unable at this meeting to make the appointment, and the matter dropped. STREET IMPROVEMENT AND HIGHWAY COMMITTEE. The minutes of this committee comprised a resolution that the following plans be approved :—Addition to house in St. James-street, Latchford, for Mr. James Strange; 12 houses in Sharp-street, for Mr. William Bostock alteration to house in Folly-lane. for Mr. John Pilling; and alteration to houses in Orford-lane, for Mr. T. Astill. The Lighting Sub-com- ,orted that they met on the 17th ult., and after

bpaotpladshfi ogr period pastod la and for the corres- sst x yearw e weeks was I£ds. 7s The minutes of the committee were adopted on the motion of the MAYOR, seconded by Councillor RIDGWAY. THE ADMISSION OF PAUPER PATIENTS INTO THE INFECTIOUS DISEASES HOSPITAL. The Sanitary Committee's minutes comprised a recom- mendation that pauper patients be not admitted into the Hospital for Infectious Diseases, and that the Town Clerk require each of the authorities having the privilege of send- ing their patients to the hospital, to forward with each case sent a written undertaking that such patient is not a pauper. Also that the probationers required from time to time at the hospital be engaged upon the following terms:—(l.) Wages to commence on engagement at the rate of £l4 per annum. (2.) After one year (subject to the recommendation of the Medical Officer), at the rate of £2O per annum. (3.) En- gagement to be subject to one month's notice of termination. It was resolved that a gratuity of £7 10s. be paid to William Bloomfield, the superintendent of the Infectious Diseases Hospital, for extra temporary services. Councillor MONKS proposed the confirmation of the minutes, which was seconded by Councillor MILNER Alderman WEBSTER asked the meaning of the recommen- dation in reference to pauper patients. Alderman HARRISON said when he read the extraordinary recommendation he could not help thinking of the various vagaries for which the committee was becoming somewhat remarkable, and he wondered what step they would take next. The committee compelled people miens volens to go into the hospital, notwithstanding there was competent medical testimony forthcoming to say that such a course was quite unnecessary. Next they found Alderman Burgess moving a resolution, which to his (Alderman Harrison's) great surprise he succeeded in carrying, making the removal of patients to the Infectious Diseases Hospital more sum- mary and arbitrary than the Act itself permitted, but which, on the advice of the Town Clerk, was rescinded as being in- operative and contrary to the spirit of the Act. That resolu- tion proposed to send people to the hospital without the intervention of a magistrate, and that of clause could not be done. (Cries of "No, no.") He was open to correction, but referred them to the resolution passed on the let February, 1881. Now, by the recommendation placed on the minutes for confirmation that night, the committee sought actually to prohibit the admission into the Infectious Diseases Hospital of that very class of persons for whom that accom- modation was most urgently required. (Hear, hear, and "No, no.") It was not very clear why they should have come to the determination to put on the minutes this recommendation because paupers had been admitted. He submitted that the recommendation could not be enteitaiued by the Council, as lie contended it was ultra vires altogether,was in opposition to the spirit of the Act of Parliament, and if passed would be inoperative. (Hear, hear.) He quoted the 26th section of the Warrington Corporation Lighting and Improvement Act to show that the committee had clearly no power to ex- clude persons in receipt of parochial relief from the advan- tages of being treated in that hospital. In proof of that he quoted Mr. Cunningham Glen's opinion, which he thought ought to be conclusive. This recommendation to exclude all persons in receipt of parochial relief from the advantages of the hospital he contended was cruel, was absurd, and in- consistent with the past professions and action of the Sani- tary Committee. He gave two instances of cruelty, and said these two cases, for the preposterous reason that the parents were receiving parochial relief, were allowed to remain in small rooms to become a radiating centre of disease that was calculated to prejudicially effect other people living in their immediate neighbourhood. One would have supposed com- mon prudence for humanity, if nothing else, would have compelled the committee at all hazards to remove these causes of disease to the hospital. But the Sanitary Com- mittee refused to entertain them at all, and said they were in receipt of parochial relief, and therefore, the workhouse authorities must deal with them. He asked who was the hospital built for—persons who could afford to provide the necessary accommodation for themselves, or for the helpless poor who had no such means at their disposal? Common sense pointed out that the hospital was intended for such people as he had referred to. ("No, no.") Both were house- holders in the borough, Slid both came under the description of the local Act, that any person shall be removed to the Infectious Diseases Hospital. (Cries of "May," and laugh- ter.) They could not discuss that question any more— . _ ndoubtedly

House. On the resumption of the Board, the following was stated to have been the business done :—Moved by Dr. McDougall, seconded by Mr. Handley, that a reply be sent to the Local Government Board stating that the Commissioners intended to utilize Waterloo House for public offices. An amend- ment wasmoved by Mr. Norman, seconded by Mr. Shaw, to the effect that a reply be sent to the Local Government litoard,.stating that the Board had not decided how they would use Waterloo House. The amendment had been carried, and was now put to the Board for confirmation. Dr. McDonueu. objected to the passing of the recom- mendation of the committee. He thought the Board had lost a golden opportunity, which might probably not occur again for many years. Not only had the Board thrown col water upon the Libraries Acts, but absolutely put a wet blanket on the formation of a library. Blr. NORMAN objected to the remark, and denied that the Board had ever opposed the establishment of a free library, or overlooked the benefits which the town would receive by the adoption of the Free Public Libraries Acts. Dr. McDoroem. was of opinion that the Board ought to do something to secure the books from the Institute. The LAW CLERK was of opinion that the Board having at last adopted plans for a new hospital, they could put Waterloo House to whatever purpose they thought proper without the sanction of the Local Government Board. Mr. HANDLEY said he was glad they had now got the mature consideration of the Law Clerk. The LAW CLERK: What is that, Mr. Handley? Mr. HANDLEY remembered that on the first day he took his seat at that Board, he observed that they were not in any way bound by the Local Government Board as to the use they should make of Waterloo House. He distinctly re- membered that the Law Clerk maintained that, without the sanction of the Local Government Board, they could not deal with Waterloo House. The Lew CLERK :_The Law Clerk did not advise any- thing of the kind. 'Me Law Clerk advised that you had no right to deal with Waterloo House until you had made some provision for the purposes for which you had bought it. You have now made those provisions, and the Local Government Board have now no claim on the house. Mr. HANDLEY maintained that the advice given by the Law Clerk was that they could not use Waterloo House for any purpose without the sanction of the Local Government Board. Now they found the Law Clerk stating that they were not bound to have their sanctim. The Lew CLERK said the Board having provided another hospital were freed from all liability. If, howeger, Mr. Handley liked to torture any advice he (the Law Clerk) might have given he could do so. Mr. HANDLEY said he was not torturing advice given. He was calling attention to the two kinds of advice they had bad. He thought all the members of the Board had the same impression. The LAW CLERK: Put the question to the members of the Board. Don't assert for them. Mr. SHAW concurred with the opinion of the Law Clerk that the Board could now deal with Waterloo House as they thought proper. The recommendation of the committee was passed, on the motion of Mr. NORMAN, seconded by Mr. WILLIAMS. The proceedings, which had lasted about two hours and a half, then terminated.

SWISS BAZAAR AT ST. lIELENS. On Wednesday, a grand Swiss bazaar was opened in the Town Hall, St. Helens. The object of the bazaar was to raise money to clear off the debt on St. Paul's Mission Church, £l,OOO being required. The Mission Church, which is situated on a piece of ground off the top part of Napier- street, was erected to meet the difficulty arising from the pew rents at St. Thomas's Church, which, it was supposed, prevented the poor from attending the services. The weekly increasing congregations show that the effort to pro- vide for the spiritual needs of that thickly populated locality has been appreciated. The church accommodates 400 persons, and all the sittings are free. Soon after the time led for opening the baraar, the Mayor (Mr. R. . . .

The following report had been laid before this committee: —" Runcorn October 31st, 1881. The Chairman of the Freeholders' 'Right Committee. Sir,—Plot of land in Weston- road, recently enclosed by Mr. John Frodsham, formerly called Box's croft, and a plot of land adjoining the Top beer- house on Runcorn Hill, which has for the last six or seven years 'been enclosed by a rail fence. I find from the town's minute book, dated August 17th, • 1838, that a number of freeholders met and laid waste as many as 66 enclosures and erections on the Common Land, such as gardens, pigsties, prides, cowhouses, &c., amongst them being one of the plots in question, viz: Cox Croft; also on the same date, 21 other encroachments were laid waste in the township of Halton, ' some of which localities are now within the Runcorn district. Again, as per minute book, dated 20th of February, 1851, a number of freeholders met the agent of the Marquis of Chol- mondeley, and proceeded to lay waste, by breaking down the fences and pulling down the walls ot 54 encroachments on Runcorn Common, amongst them being the two plots in question, viz: Cox's Croft and gardens at the Top beerhouse. Israel Thompson, stonemason, says that be has lived at Higher Runcorn 58 Years, that he remembers the plot of land now enclosed by -John Frodsharn being occupied by John Cox (then living on Mill-brow) who grew potatoes, ..t7c., en it. The plot of land was then wailed round and Cox paid a rent of some amount to the Mar quis of Cholmondeley for thr same. Cox held this plot until about 1851, when a numbee of freeholders met and broke down the fences of this land and many other enclosures, amongs them being the gardens now adjoining CAley's cottage, opposite the water works. These, however, he says, were reinstated in a few days, and have not since been interfered with. He also says that Geo. Moulton (now living in One of the cottages in question), had to do with the enclosing f the gardens at the time, and very likely would be able to give soma in- formation. He further states that the portion adjoining the Tup beerhouse has been enclosed within the last six years by Thomas Hindley, who then kept the said beerhouse. titled to go into the hospital. Councillor PIERPOINT supported the amendment. He considered all ratepayers had a right to go into the hospital. Councillor MONKS, in replying, said the speakers had con- fined themselves to Warrington, whereas the resolution applied to many other districts, and if they passed the amendment they would to some extent confine the hands of the committee in reference to other districts in which arrangements had been made. (" No, no.") Alderman Harrison was chairman of the Board of Guardians who were seeking through his efforts to throw the responsibility of the maintenance of pauper patients upon the town. That was really the gist of the whole thing. Whether the Coun- cil would supwlrt any such scheme remained to be seen. Alderman Harrison was very loud in his praises of or people, but he condemned the inmates of Workhouses as the very scum of the earth as a rule. Were these the class of people they would care to introduce into a hospital where they had to send their own children, and where they were liable to send their own wives and even go themselves? He could not see why the Guardians—for it was manifestly their duty—neglected to make provision for their sick, and the Sanitary Committee was doing its duty in calling upon I them to make that provision. Alderman DAVIES asked the Town Clerk to repeat his statement that the Guardians possessed sufficient power to require patients to go into the House. The TOWN CLERK: I am quite sure that they have that power in all cases corning within the provisions of the Public Health Act. Councillor JEANS : Will you give me your authority. (Loud cries of "Oh.") The amendment was then put, when there voted for it: Aldermen Harrison, Webster, Kean ; Councillors Mackie, I Sutton, Woolfall, Taylor, Burgess, Jeans, Francomb, Ash- ton, and Dixon. For the resolution there voted: The Mayor, Aldermen Holmes, Davies; Councillors Whittle, Crosfield, Monks, Ridgway, Milner, Platt, Brown, Litton, Barker, I Wallington, and Caldwell. The minutes were therefore passed by 14 votes to 12. TIIE GAS COMMITTEE. The minutes of this committee contained a recommenda- tion that the price of coke be advanced to Bs. 44. per ton; that the tender of Mr. W. Winstanley for the white- washing, papering, ctic., of six cottages in Coronation Build- ings, and the painting of two cottages in Academy street, be accepted; that the contract now existing with Messrs. I Me idows and Son for the purchase of tar, and which would , expire on the 30th June, 1882, be terminated on the 31st December next, and that a fresh contract be entered into with Messrs. Meadows and Son for the purchase of all surplus tar for two years, commencing on the Ist January, 1882, at the price of 355. per ton. Alderman HourEs moved, and Councillor MILNER secon- ded, the confirmation of the minutes, which was carried. TIIE FLOODS PREVENTION BILL. Councillor CROSFIELD moved the passing of the minutes of the Rivers Committee,and Alderman DAVIES, in seconding the motion, said a deputation from the committee had waited upon the Salford Corporation with regard to the Rivers Conservancy Floods Prevention Bill. They were agreed as to the desirability of passing the Bill, but would endeavour to get struck out those clauses which were inimical to the interests of Salford and Warrington. The Salford Corpora- tion would wait upon Mr. Dodson, the President of the Local Government Board, the next day, and he (Mr. Davies) would then have an opportunity of supporting the Bill. The minutes were passed. MR. REAMONT'S PORTRAIT. The General Purposes Committee at their meeting passed a minute' that the Borough Surveyor submitted his report as to the beet means to be adopted to prevent flooding in Howley, which, after consideration, was ordered to be entered on the minutes.—Recommended, that the Borough Surveyor be instructed to request the owners of the pro- perty adjoining the brooks in and near Howley to meet this committee, with the object of making arrangements with them for permanently preventing the occurrence of floods in Howley.—The Borough Surveyor submitted a plan showing proposed formation of aniinproved road to Arpley, under the L. Jr N. W. R. Co.'s iron bridge, and it was resolved that he invite the representatives of the •Arpley land owners to meet this committee to see how thework can be conveniently carried out.—Resolved, that the following members be ap- pointed a sub-committee to act as a Parliamentary Com- mittee, the Mayor, convener; Aldermen Burgess, Holmes, Davies, and Webster, and Councillors Fairclongh and Milner. —Resolved, that the following members be appointed a sub-committee to report to the committee as to the most ap- propriate places to be secured by the Corporation for the pur- pose of forming open spaces and recreation grounds in the borough : The Mayor, Aldermen Holmes, Davies, and Kean, and Councillor Broadbent. The MAYOR, in moving the adoption of the minutes, re- marked that the portrait of Mr. Beamont, the first mayor of Warrington, had been removed into the Council Chamber in consequence of the redeooration of the Mayor's Parlour, and he should like an expression of opinion from the Council as to its remaining in the Council Chamber. Mr. Beamont thought it looked better in its present position. After a short discussion a show of hands was taken, and, with the exception of Alderman Webster, the members were in favour of the portrait remaining in the Council Chamber. Alderman HARRISON seconded the adoption of the minutes, which were passed. HARMsTON'S CIRCUS. The MAYOR read a letter from Mr. Harinston soliciting the patronage and presence of the Mayor and Council at his Circus on some evening. He would give half the gross receipts to the Infirmary. (Hear, hear.) The invitation met with general approval, but the date of the visit was not fixed. lad- I
